author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Yasmine Benabderrahmane
title: Is "khawa khawa" a North African myth?
content:
In the haze of

el ghorba

 — the strangeness and alienation of living abroad — I gravitate toward the Maghrebi diaspora. For a moment, we relax our tongues from the unnatural twists of Arabic dialects foreign to us and speak in the Maghrebi

darija

s. Desperate to latch onto whatever whispers of home exist elsewhere, we claim that we are

khawa khawa

.

Among the Algerians, Moroccans, and Tunisians,

khawa khawa

 is an official nod to an unofficial alliance, loosely translating to

brotherhood

. It is an ode to our shared cultures and history in the face of North African identity discourses.

But what began as a salve for colonialism was lost in the monotonous chants for brotherhood.

Before the 19th century, North African states were “undefined” to European cartographers and authorities alike. Hence, like the concept of the Middle East and the Sahel, the Maghreb was prone to imperial invention. Unsurprisingly, this coincided with the Scramble for Africa — when the insatiable greed of European colonial powers took interest in dividing the African continent among themselves.

Encompassing other colonial legacies, the borders born out of the Scramble engineered the ethnic rivalries that persist in Africa today. Through the newly devised borders and the infamous “divide and conquer” regimes, the Maghreb was branded as distinct.

Despite the existing racial diversity of the region, the French colonial regimes rebranded the Maghreb as a biracial society: Amazigh or Arab. While the Amazigh identity was mislabeled in proximity to the whiteness of Europe, the Arab identity became an accusation of settler colonialism. North Africa became a geographic body for the Francophonie world, distanced from its neighboring regions’ cultures, politics, and society.

In 1962, Algeria — the last of France’s Maghrebi colonies — declared independence. In the years that followed, the Maghrebi people looked inwards and toward rebuilding the identity of North Africa. Thus,

khawa khawa

 was born and reinforced by the diaspora that fled their homes in the wake of political instability. It became a card dealt in moments of desperation to bond to something, or someone, that vaguely resembled home.

Khawa khawa

, and the brotherhood that blossomed with it, became the means to redress an identity obscured by European colonialism.

True

khawa khawa

 culture demands communal harmony void of ego. But when politics becomes inevitably entangled in the national identity of communities, the culture of Maghrebi brotherhood falls flat.

Shortly after 1962, newly independent Algeria and Morocco fell into border disputes. The following decades spiraled into attempted land grabs, fits of cultural monopolies, and accusations of expansionist ambitions. In response, the people cried out

khawa khawa; our governments do not define our brotherhood

!

But too often, the politics override the social bonds of Algerians and Moroccans (and occasionally, Tunisians). With the rise of the internet, discourse shifted, and social media became a useful mirror for the abstractions of the Maghrebi identity.

Most recently, the

khawa khawa

 culture was dramatically pronounced dead on social media platforms, following the 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON). Almost overnight, the football tournament became a litmus test for Algerian-Moroccan relations and spiraled into a warped perception of North African relations. A futile online back-and-forth that began as shared banter turned into personal attacks and political scrutiny.

The post-AFCON

guerre

 between Algerians and Moroccans — which coincided with the recent

UN support

 for Moroccan plans over the Western Sahara, disapproved by the Algerian government — is a recurring phenomenon of how Maghrebi culture wages war parallel to the political tensions of its respective countries. Despite the adamant denial, online Maghrebi communities fall into the habit of using our governments to verify the authenticity of

khawa khawa

.

The problem rests in the fact that both communities — Algerian and Moroccan — fall into the habit of claiming the minority of hateful comments as the consensus among the entirety of both nations. We see assertions made that we cannot prove, except that they are too insulting and their wounds far too inflicting to recover from. It has become a pattern of malice between both nations that resurfaces regardless of how loudly

khawa khawa

 is chanted.

Perhaps the fault is also in the fragility …

author: Mike Ludwig
title: In Virginia, Racism and Redlining Are Fueling a Flock Camera Backlash
content:
Police in Hampton Roads saturated Black and low-income neighborhoods with Flock-style cameras, a study found.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Local governments in Virginia are under mounting pressure to cancel contracts for surveillance cameras known as automated license plate readers (ALPRs). On October 6, the Henrico County Police Division announced that it would terminate its contract for such cameras after residents shared “legitimate concerns about Flock Safety.” In nearby Richmond, Mayor Danny Avula said on October 13 that the city would cancel its contract with Flock Safety, the most famous purveyor of the cameras, but did not rule out using ALPRs from a different company.

“It is a good first step, but we do need to keep the pressure on the city to not automatically switch to another ALPR vendor,” Richmond Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member Victoria McCullough told Truthout.

DSA activists and residents in Richmond pushing police to ditch the contract have powerful research to point to from elsewhere in the state. In the neighboring Hampton Roads region of Virginia, race and class are the primary predictors of locations where police installed ALPRs, a groundbreaking study found earlier this year.

The study found police were more likely to install ALPRs in majority Black census tracts in each of the nine cities across the Hampton Roads region, an East Coast metroplex with 1.8 million residents and multiple cities, including Norfolk and Virginia Beach. About 80 percent of majority Black neighborhoods contain at least one camera compared to fewer than 40 percent of majority white tracts. ALPR surveillance is also more intense in majority Black neighborhoods, where on average there are four times as many cameras than in white neighborhoods when weighted for population share.

In Virginia Beach, police deployed ALPRs in only five of 76 majority white census tracts (6.6 percent), compared to one of two Black census tracts (50 percent). Black residents of the locality are 7.6 times more likely than white residents to live in a census tract with at least one ALPR. When weighted for the number of cameras deployed in each area, Black drivers in Virginia Beach were roughly eight times more likely than white drivers to be regularly surveilled by Flock-style cameras.

Published in January 2026, the study found a “similarly consistent pattern of disproportionate camera coverage” in low-income areas and concluded that ALPR deployment in Hampton Roads follows historical patterns of housing discrimination, racist segregation, and disinvestment. In other words, police have deployed the cameras so Black and lower-income people are more likely to live under high-tech, AI-powered traffic surveillance than whiter, wealthier people.

Dr. Steven Keener is a co-author of the study and director of the Center for Crime, Equity and Justice Research at Christopher Newport University. He pointed to Norfolk State University in Norfolk, one of only five historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) in Virginia, as an example of the increased surveillance presence. The area in and around the university is heavily saturated with Flock brand ALPR cameras, compared to whiter and higher-income areas of Norfolk, the study found.

“The census tract with the most ALPR cameras surrounds Norfolk State, which is the only public HBCU in the region,” Keener told Truthout in an interview. “The cameras completely encircle the campus, so you can’t enter or exit in a vehicle without being surveilled.”

Of the census tracts with the highest number of ALPRs, nine are located in Norfolk, where the cameras are concentrated in historically Black neighborhoods and near public housing. The ALPR data used in the study was only available because a federal judge ordered police to release the records in November 2025 as part of a privacy rights lawsuit filed by two residents of Norfolk. Keener’s team used the data to map out ALPR locations across Hampton Roads and compare the results to Census data on race and income.

“Economic and social policy failures have led to your life being constantly surveilled,” Keener said of lower-income and Black communities. “They’re still doing racialized surveillance and policing, but instead of having an officer on the corner, they are watching you to criminalize your behavior based on where you …

author: By L. Cam Anderson, Contributor
title: How The Proud Boys Lost Their Name
content:
West Palm Beach, FL – On Sept. 26, the film “American Martyrs” premiered at the Kravis Center’s Cohen Pavilion in West Palm Beach, Florida. 


The subject of the film, presented by the far-right media outlet Gateway Pundit, was the Proud Boys – specifically the “seditious five,” whom a federal jury found guilty of seditious conspiracy to stop the presidential transfer of power for their role in the Jan. 6, 2021 storming of the U.S. Capitol.


The official poster for the film, promoted by Enrique Tarrio and Gateway Pundit on X ahead of its premiere. Note that Zachary Rehl, first on the left in the lineup, is AI-generated.


The five Proud Boys presenting the film were chairman Henry “Enrique” Tarrio, Ethan Nordean, Joe Biggs, Zachary Rehl and Dominic Pezzola. In reality, the actual fifth member of the “seditious five” is Jeremy Bertino, not Pezzola, who pleaded guilty and testified against the others during their trial. 


In August 2025, Bertino appeared on an episode of Tarrio’s Substack podcast titled “Kiss of Judas,” where the “government star witness” allowed the permanently sunglasses-clad chairman to humiliate him for the twelve people who liked the post. Despite this entreaty to re-enter the flock, Bertino did not make the cut as an “American martyr.”


Besides Tarrio, who received a full pardon, the others had the sentences commuted by executive order during President Donald Trump’s first day back in office on Jan. 20, 2025. 


The film premiere, held less than four miles from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club, was graced by numerous right-wing characters, including leading “Stop the Steal” figure and former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani,

QAnon digital warrior

 and former U.S. Army general Michael Flynn and convicted fraudster George Santos.


Led by right-wing media figure Lara Logan, the event opened at 7 p.m. with an open bar that overlapped with a 10-minute window set aside for “prayer, national anthem and pledge.”


After the 80-minute film concluded, the Gateway Pundit presented Tarrio with a Gateway Pundit-branded award created specifically for the occasion recognizing him “as an American Martyr and Hero.”


“It’s not an Emmy,” Tarrio wrote on X two days later. “But it’s so much better.”


[Source: Enrique Tarrio on X]


Despite the obvious connections to the Proud Boys organization, the premiere lacked any of the recognizable branding belonging to what it depicted as a persecuted “drinking fraternity.”


Even on Tarrio’s person, the golden cock and abbreviated name have given way to the branding for his streaming outfit, “War Boys,” which has gained a whopping 700 followers on Rumble since the channel was created in April last year.


And on Tarrio’s merch website – where the Afro-Cuban now in his 40s markets just about any idea as apparel, including a t-shirt reading “Enrique Tarrio Eats Cream Pies” with an AI illustration of Tarrio licking an over-sized cream pie – reveals a distinct absence of Proud Boys related merchandise.


[Source: Enrique Tarrio on X]


Tarrio’s ability to capitalize on Proud Boys merchandising, which once characterized his merch store, hit a setback last year when a D.C. Superior Court judge awarded the brand to a historically-Black church following a years-long legal battle set in the wake of the 2020 Presidential election.


At the beginning of 2025, the Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal (MAME) church was the only place one could purchase official Proud Boys merchandise, re-branded to signify Black pride, with proceeds going toward the church’s community justice fund.


In April 2025, the church’s hold on the brand was tested on the Hudson Valley Proud Boys, who were sued in the Southern District Court of New York for their continued usage of the Proud Boys branding and merchandising.


The court reached a default judgment against the Hudson Valley Proud Boys, a chapter associated with Tarrio, earlier this year on April 8, awarding MAME $75,000 for trademark infringement and nearly $200,000 in attorney’s fees.


The judgment against the Hudson Valley Proud Boys is only a small part of the church’s pursuit to be fully compensated in the amount awarded by the court, which continues to be a major struggle to this day and sees all related parties continue to be wrapped up in the ongoing court battle.


On the night of Dec. 12, 2020, the streets of Washington were thronged with black shirts and red caps.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Iqaluit woman charged with 2nd-degree murder
content:
RCMP have charged a woman with second-degree murder following a disturbance in Iqaluit’s Tundra Valley neighbourhood over the weekend.


Police found a 37-year-old woman with life threatening injuries in the city’s 2400 block at around 5:50 a.m. on Saturday, said RCMP spokesperson Sgt. George Henrie in a news release.


She was transported to Qikiqtani General hospital, where she died.


Christie Nutarariaq, 32, has been charged with second degree murder in relation to the incident.


The incident is unrelated to

another

 murder charge that police announced Monday.


In that case, RCMP charged a 21-year-old Qaqasie Aningmiuq with second-degree murder, following an altercation on Oct. 6 that left one man dead.


Nutarariaq is in custody. Her next court appearance is set for Nov. 17.

author: Jolene Banning
title: My ancestors showed me how to grieve
content:
Jolene Banning’s daughter Amber-baa, depicted through the eye of an eagle. Illustration by Jessie Boulard


Content warning: This story deals with child loss and grief. Please look after your spirit and read with care


Three years ago I was hit with a pain so deep that it seared through every fiber of my body. 


Two police officers pulled up in my driveway, driving a dark SUV, wearing dark suits and ties. They came to inform me that my child, my baby, my daughter Amber had died. 


The blow of information left me numb, stunned, separated from myself like I was watching this happen instead of partaking. 


Instantly, I became a member of a club I never wanted to belong to: of parents who have lost their children. Because I know I’m not alone in this rapidly growing group of people. It doesn’t feel natural to bury our children, so young, so beautiful. 


Amber-baa had long, shiny dark brown hair, round brown eyes, thick eyebrows and a million dollar smile — which she should, considering how much I paid the orthodontist. She was warm, caring, and fun to be around. She lit up a room and made sure everyone felt seen. And in the blink of an eye, without warning, I had lost all of that. The silence was deafening. The pain was inescapable. 


Experiencing this kind of loss and grief is not uncommon for Indigenous people. In “Canada,” our communities experience significantly higher mortality rates. Our women and girls are at a 12 times higher risk than the average citizen to go missing or be murdered.


Violence against us is fuelled by systemic racism, sexism, and colonialism — as outlined in

Reclaiming Power and Place, the Final Report of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls

.


We hear about these losses. Sometimes it makes the news, stats are shared, but then we don’t hear from anyone again. The news has passed, new topics are making headlines. 


Losing my daughter, and losing other important people in my life too soon, led me to want to acknowledge this and share my reality, and I grapple with how we can begin to heal. 


My first loss came when I was only 13. My baby brother was only six months old and died of meningitis after spending a week in the Toronto Hospital for Sick Children. After that, I would go on to lose many of my aunties, uncles and cousins, and grandparents. 


Many lives shut down before they even reached their prime.


“For these four days, my pain was spread out amongst everyone at the fire.”


When I lost my girl, on April 28th, 2023, there was no way I was sending her on her next journey in a way that was not ours — in a church made of brick and mortar while someone delivered a sermon about finding God and peace. 


So I turned to my Anishinaabek community and found knowledge holders and learners willing to share with me. 


I was told I need to send my girl off with a four-day sacred fire ceremony, something I had never done or even participated in until this loss. 


I called the Elders that I knew, and many people worked behind the scenes to ensure I had enough fire wood, food, and company. Firekeepers attended to the fire and explained which direction to enter, drum groups stopped by and offered songs. 


Every morning, as the sun rose, my dad was there, sharing family stories. Relatives from the north made the trek to offer medicine, condolences and stories of their own.


Another community member, who lost a child, offered to make my daughter a headstone. It’s a simple cross, with her information, and features a painted medicine wheel. 


For these four days, my pain was spread out amongst everyone at the fire.


I also learned during this ceremony that my daughter needed to start her journey and there were ways I could assist her. 


She needed her own bundle with exactly four matchsticks, a copper cup, an outfit made in her colours so our ancestors can recognize her and moccasins — basic and unembellished ones, since our offerings grow in size when they reach the other dimension, realm, Spirit World, and we don’t want her weighed down, unable to walk. 


I was told she will come to a crossing, where she will have to share everything about herself and her journey so far. Then our ancestors will travel across the divide to accept her. Her bundle was packed just right.


Every day and every night over four days we feasted for her by offering a spirit plate to the land, another to the fire. 


In Anishinaabek culture, we add the prefix -baa onto a name …

author: Kevin Carson
title: Review. CLR James: Cultivator of the Popular Will, by Matthew Quest
content:
Matthew Quest.

CLR James: Cultivator of the Popular Will. A Study of the History and Politics of World Revolution

 (Brill, 2026).


As Matthew Quest notes in his appendix, “Top Ten Reasons We Don’t Know More about CLR James,” CLR James is a relatively obscure thinker even among the African-American left. This is doubly so on the left more generally. According to Quest, James’ thought occupies a marginal position on the left primarily because his fundamental orientation — an affinity for direct democracy and workers’ self-management — is fundamentally at odds with the centralized, mass-based politics of the Old Left, whether Marxist-Leninist or Social Democratic. He was hostile to the British Labour Party and Atlee, the US Democratic Party and FDR, and to post-independence African leaders who were lionized elsewhere on the left. He saw nation-states and vanguard parties as mostly destructive rather than helpful, and the history of nationalization by progressive governments as hostile to self-management. James also saw the class reductionism of the dominant currents of the left, with their neglect of racial and anti-colonial dimensions of struggle, as failing to meet the needs of the time.


Quest himself is a perfect fit for intellectual biographer of James, as a historian and critic of national liberation movements in Africa and elsewhere in the colonial and post-colonial world, as well as post-independence governments. James’ central values of direct democracy and self-governance resonate strongly with Quest’s hostility — which come through clearly in these quotes from his Preface — to self-serving establishments, Black, revolutionary, and/or “progressive.”


The search for identity and heritage, in all their proper cultural nuances, for those who have known scars, exploitation, and who are overcoming insecurity, cannot be permitted to be captured by those who define freedom as managing subordinate lives. This is how all who fatefully embrace the state define it. These are the facts of the long duration of post-civil rights, post-colonial existence.


…Hopefully, we have now learned that the challenge to respectability politics without opposition to elite representative government is a fraud….


We are living in an affirmative action empire and ethnically plural police state alongside subcontractors of guilt and activists for the government, funded by the white rich, talking about privilege. We have people lecturing us about the problem of ‘colour blindness’ who are not opposed to the police state; they are explicitly part of the boss class who murder, mass incarcerate, and get out the vote for those who exploit.


* * *


…[W]hen I questioned whether the working people of Cuba actually governed that country, many dedicated revolutionaries, socialists, and anti- imperialists replied that it did not matter. For most insulted by the historical denial of self-determination of conquered peoples and for most organising for some future socialism or communism, it did not matter whether ordinary people directly governed or not. This should shake those who are not Machiavellians to the core. We should not be so thirsty for empowerment that we will accept a half-made or second-hand society as a dwelling to sustain our search for liberation.


…No workers or youth to whom we were introduced asked questions about their contradictions. Surely, ordinary people in Cuba asked these questions but were not featured on the directed tours and cultural events. This raised questions about the democratic content and the political economy of the socialist future and the ethics of those who took part in such projects.


* * *


CLR James famously said: ‘Political treachery is not the monopoly of the white race’. He also said there are Black people who treat Black toilers like ‘colonial trustees’, and while they talk of desiring ‘independence’ and ‘power’ they already live a ‘delightful’ existence at the toilers’ expense.


James’ life (1901-1989) spanned the Russian Revolution, the rise and fracturing of Marxism-Leninism, and postwar national liberation movements, and intersected with them at numerous points.


Born in Trinidad, he lived in numerous countries over the course of his lifetime. His activist career was wide-ranging and global; as Quest writes, “James and his associates worked for an American revolution, a Caribbean revolution, African revolution, and world revolution.” He authored numerous historical works, including

The …

author: Halie Moses
title: The Z Factor: Young Voters and the 2026 Midterms
content:
Generation Z voters (aged 18-29) are predicted to make a significant impact on the upcoming 2026 Midterm elections. This has not always been the case, as student and youth voter turnout has historically remained low. Only 47% of Americans aged 18-29 voted in the 2024 election. This year, 50 million Gen Z Americans are eligible to vote.

In October, a report by UCLA’s William Institute examined the political priorities and voting intentions of Gen Z adults ahead of the 2026 midterms. The study found that nearly 74 percent of respondents said they were likely or certain to vote. These numbers come as no surprise to those who work with students, spend time organizing on college campuses, or identify as Gen Z during the Trump Administration. Rising living costs, ICE raids, attacks on reproductive rights access, sexual assault cases, climate change, and unwanted wars have directly impacted their lives and are driving them to the polls with a passion for change.

Leela Strong, Director of CIRCLE, who works to empower the youth vote, reflected: “Young people are sending us clear signals, not only of dissatisfaction with our politics and deep economic concerns, but also of a strong desire to take action and drive change.” Organizations such as When We All Vote are working to engage young people by connecting their priorities with the issues and candidates on their ballots. Opportunities to participate alongside friends and classmates can also encourage young people to become more involved in politics.

Campus organizing is another part of these efforts. The Feminist Majority Foundation’s Feminist Campus program is actively working to get the student vote out. Students can help their peers register to vote, understand their ballot, and march to the polls in solidarity. These efforts are particularly important for first-time voters, who may need guidance.

Not only are young people planning to vote, but they are also planning to vote overwhelmingly Democratic. In the September Economist/YouthGov Poll, when asked who they will cast their ballot for, 54% of 18-29-year-olds said the Democratic candidate, compared with 22% who said the Republican candidate. The same survey found a sentiment among youth that reflects that the Republican Party is too extreme. When asked, “Do you think the Republican Party is too extreme?” 65% of 18- 29-year-olds replied yes. In contrast, only 29% believe the Democratic Party is too extreme. These results reflect the views of respondents at the time of the survey and do not necessarily predict how young people will vote in November.

These numbers are significant and show promising signs that young people are empowered to change the course of our political and social reality. Voter registration, accessible election information, and campus organizing can help young people navigate the voting process and participate in decisions that affect their futures. To learn more, head to vote411.org/feminist.

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in

New York

,

California

, and

Illinois

 — have

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022,

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 


But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 


Disability justice organization HEARD points out that

it’s

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in

state

 and

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.


Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC)

distributed tablets

 to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).  


In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.


“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a

press release

 announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”


There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the

complaint

 filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist. 


“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told

Truthout

. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.” 


IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.


Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC

announced

 it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release,

IDOC said

 that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.” 


But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs. 


Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint. 


“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”


The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.


“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”


These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.


“In prisons where we’ve seen scores of deaf/disabled people, there may only be 2 videophones,” Kah Mendoza, the communications coordinator for

HEARD

, told …

author: Alison Avigayil Ramer
title: After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces
content:
This article

After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Since the massacres on Oct. 7, now three years ago, the news has brought a steady stream of horror and broken promises. The ceasefire in Gaza has been broken thousands of times; the ceasefire with Iran only holds until the next strike. Many of us have responded by going numb or turning away. Over these three years, I’ve come to believe that collective mourning can help movements build sturdier organizing infrastructure, move through paralysis and numbness, and get back to the long-term work of creating systemic change.


I’ve spent nearly two decades living and working as a human rights defender, mostly in Palestine and Israel. For years, I responded to atrocities the way much of the dominant organizing culture did at the time: strategically. I prepared statements, launched campaigns and mobilized our base. I worked through several wars and the ongoing ethnic cleansing and genocide. Even though my colleagues and I were often physically together, we rarely had the opportunity to collectively mourn. In fact, mourning was often seen as something only the privileged could afford. As organizers and solidarity activists, we were the ones who needed to push past the pain and keep mobilizing.


And then, after each war, large swaths of colleagues and organizers would burn out, and our movement would suffer a setback. Movement researchers Paul Gorski and Cher Chen, studying U.S. human rights and social justice activists, found that an estimated 50 to 60 percent of organizers eventually walk away from movement work and never return, burned out by a culture that treats overwork and self-sacrifice as necessary. That culture also leaves no room to mourn and process the secondary trauma that accumulates, hastening burnout. These kinds of cycles make it especially hard for movements seeking systemic change to sustain themselves.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


When Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023 and I was waiting in anticipation of the retaliation against Gaza, I knew I couldn’t respond with the same kind of organizing strategy that we usually use: preparation of advocacy statements, social media campaigns and fundraising appeals. I knew that while some people should and would continue that work, there also needed to be spaces for organizers and our base to mourn. And so, on Oct. 8, I opened a space for collective mourning online, sharing it in the many community, political and religious groups I was a part of, for anyone who needed somewhere to process what they were witnessing and feeling. Dozens of people joined: primarily my Jewish community at first, and then people from many faiths and chapters of my life, from Palestine to Palo Alto. 


As the assault on Gaza and the genocide continued, the room stayed open. More colleagues, including community organizers, artists, chaplains and psychologists, joined me in facilitating, and we held space for hundreds of people from across our communities to mourn together. We formed a collective called the

Social Change Sanctuary

 and developed a format that included facilitation and participation from attendees. Over time, we were invited to hold spaces for other communities in mourning. We’ve held spaces to grieve the ongoing genocide; climate catastrophes like the fires in Los Angeles; ICE raids, arrests and murders; and the war on Iran.


The Social Change Sanctuary hosts an Interdependence Day circle in 2025. (Alison Avigayil Ramer)


Participants repeatedly shared the difference it made in their lives to know they had a consistent space to mourn.


“In daily life, when something hurts, I turn away, I distract myself,” one participant told us. “But the collective mourning practice helped me move through the frozenness that constant news induced — helped me stop doomscrolling — and I’m able to return to my work.”


That participant went on to organize her community and raised $20,000 for refugees in Gaza. 


Another participant returned to their role as a chaplain, and extended her work to include “movement chaplaincy” holding one-on-one spaces for people doing solidarity work. 


Many participants also shared how witnessing the news with others enabled them to feel the emotions provoked by the headlines, leaving them feeling less isolated and more connected. That is co-regulation happening at …

author: anred
title: UNICEF advierte que 60mil niños y niñas perdieron a uno o ambos padres en el genocidio contra Gaza
content:
A más de un año del anuncio del alto el fuego, la infancia palestina continúa pagando las consecuencias de la guerra. Un nuevo informe de UNICEF alerta sobre las muertes, los desplazamientos y el impacto psicológico que atraviesan cientos de miles de niños y niñas en la Franja de Gaza. Pero lo terrible es la cifra confirmada por el organización internacional: 60 niños perdieron a uno o ambos padres. Mientras más de 20 mil niños fueron asesinados (340 a pesar del alto al fuego) y otros 44 mil heridos registrados solo hasta eoctubre del 2025. Por ANRed


Unos 60.000 niños y niñas de Gaza perdieron a uno o ambos progenitores durante la guerra o desde el anuncio del alto el fuego. La cifra fue difundida por UNICEF el 16 de octubre, en un nuevo informe que expone las consecuencias de la ofensiva israelí sobre la población infantil palestina.


El organismo también informó que alrededor de 800.000 menores continúan desplazados y que muchos sobreviven en carpas precarias o edificios bombardeados que representan un riesgo para su seguridad. El acceso limitado a servicios esenciales, la destrucción de sus hogares y la pérdida de familiares profundizan una crisis que no terminó con la declaración de la tregua.


El impacto de la violencia también continúa reflejándose en las víctimas. Según UNICEF, más de 340 niños y niñas murieron y cientos resultaron heridos durante el período transcurrido desde el anuncio del alto el fuego, en octubre de 2025. Durante las dos semanas previas al nuevo informe, se reportaron menores muertos y heridos por ataques aéreos, drones y disparos.


La pérdida de madres y padres no implica solamente el duelo: también deja a miles de chicos y chicas en situaciones de extrema vulnerabilidad económica, social y emocional. UNICEF advierte que la infancia necesita protección, atención psicológica, alimentación, acceso a la salud y condiciones seguras para reconstruir sus vidas.


Mientras los niños asesinados también fueron documentados por UNICEf aunque advierte que la cifra puede ser mayor:


Al menos 20 179 niños

 murieron y más de 44 143 resultaron heridos como consecuencia directa de las hostilidades en Gaza entre el 7 de octubre de 2023 y octubre de 2025, según un informe de una comisión de investigación de la ONU publicado en junio de 2026.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Albigasta en lucha: el agua no se negocia frente al avance de la megaminería
content:
Vecinos de Santiago del Estero y Catamarca resisten el proyecto de litio El Alto y denuncian los riesgos para las cuencas hídricas. Cerca de 50 impugnaciones cuestionaron la consulta pública. La disputa expone las contradicciones de los gobiernos provinciales y de un modelo extractivista que el Gobierno de Milei busca profundizar con el RIGI y el Súper RIGI.


Por Adrián Flores para Red Eco


Frías, Santiago Del Estero / Sierras De Ancasti, Catamarca


El agua que da vida a las comunidades de la Región Albigasta está en el centro de una creciente disputa. Mientras los gobiernos de Santiago del Estero y Catamarca anuncian obras para mejorar el abastecimiento de agua potable mediante el Acueducto Albigasta, el proyecto minero El Alto genera preocupación por sus posibles efectos sobre las cuencas hídricas de las Sierras de Ancasti.


Las asambleas socioambientales y los vecinos autoconvocados cuestionan el avance de la exploración de litio a cargo de Litios del Norte S.A. y reclaman información pública, controles independientes y garantías para proteger el agua, los bosques nativos y el patrimonio cultural de la región.


Además,  los pobladores de la Región de Albigasta advierten que la empresa Litios del Norte S.A  amenaza con ingresar con sus vehículos a la zona de exploración, acompañada de la policía y la gendarmería.


La contradicción es evidente: se anuncian inversiones públicas para garantizar el acceso al agua mientras se impulsa una actividad privada cuyos posibles impactos sobre ese mismo recurso deben ser rigurosamente evaluados.


La Respuesta de los Pueblos: Organización y Resistencia


Según informó El Ancasti el 28 de septiembre de 2026, la Asamblea de Ancasti por la Vida, la Asamblea Friense y vecinos autoconvocados presentaron cerca de 50 impugnaciones ante la Dirección Provincial de Gestión Ambiental Minera, cuestionando las condiciones de la consulta pública del proyecto. La charla informativa prevista para el 30 de septiembre fue suspendida.


Posteriormente, el 18 de octubre, el mismo medio informó que el senador departamental Rodolfo Santillán y el intendente de Ancasti, Randolfo Piñero, solicitaron suspender preventivamente las tareas de exploración hasta contar con una Declaración de Impacto Ambiental aprobada y garantías de participación ciudadana.


Las comunidades advierten sobre un proyecto que, según la información difundida por los sectores movilizados, abarcaría más de 34.000 hectáreas, con perforaciones de hasta 300 metros de profundidad, a unos nueve kilómetros del dique El Bolsón. También cuestionan un consumo de agua atribuido a la documentación ambiental que alcanzaría los 2.100.000 litros durante una etapa de exploración. Estas cifras deben cotejarse con los expedientes y estudios técnicos completos.


Las preguntas siguen abiertas: ¿de dónde se extraerá el agua?, ¿qué riesgos existen para las reservas subterráneas?, ¿qué controles se realizarán y quién responderá ante eventuales daños?


La preocupación también alcanza al bosque nativo y al patrimonio arqueológico, incluido el Parque Arqueológico La Tunita. Las autoridades deben publicar los estudios y permisos correspondientes, responder las objeciones y garantizar que la participación comunitaria no sea un mero trámite administrativo.


Milei, el Rigi y el Súper Rigi: Más Privilegios para el gran capital


El conflicto de Albigasta no puede separarse del modelo económico nacional. El Gobierno de Javier Milei impulsa políticas destinadas a atraer grandes inversiones extractivas y exportadoras. El Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones (RIGI), establecido por la Ley 27.742, concede beneficios fiscales, aduaneros y cambiarios a proyectos que cumplan determinados requisitos.


En mayo de 2026, el Gobierno anunció el denominado Súper RIGI, una propuesta de ampliación de incentivos para nuevas inversiones industriales. Su alcance debe distinguirse de las disposiciones vigentes, pero vuelve a poner sobre la mesa una discusión central: ¿quién se beneficia con la explotación de los bienes naturales y quién carga con sus consecuencias?


Desde una perspectiva socioambiental crítica, estos regímenes profundizan un modelo que privilegia la rentabilidad empresarial y las exportaciones, mientras las comunidades reclaman agua segura, trabajo digno y protección territorial.


El capitalismo, en su lógica de acumulación ilimitada y subordinación de la naturaleza a la ganancia, es incompatible con la defensa de la vida cuando convierte …

author: Caio Barretto Briso
title: Silêncio de Flávio sobre Ana Clara “foi desesperador”, diz a mãe da menina
content:
Naquele 2 de fevereiro de 2021, a família de Cristiane tinha acabado de acordar e seus dois filhos, a menina com cinco e Pedro com dois anos, estavam brincando na porta de casa. De repente, dois disparos. Cristiane correu e, ao chegar onde as crianças estavam, viu um policial parado diante de Ana Clara. Ele deu vários tiros para o alto sem dizer nada. Não quis nem prestar socorro, só o fez após outro policial se aproximar e dizer “pega a garota que você fez merda”.


“Então ele carregou ela de qualquer jeito, pra não manchar a farda de sangue. Tirei minha filha dos braços dele e levei no meu colo. Ela não chorava, não gemia, não gritava. Perto do hospital, abriu os olhos e desceu uma lagrimazinha do olho dela. Pra mim, ela morreu ali”, lembra Cristiane Gomes da Silva, que também era quase uma criança quando Ana Clara nasceu – tinha 15 anos de idade.


Nesta segunda-feira, 19 de outubro, dia seguinte ao debate da Band entre o presidente Lula e o senador

Flávio Bolsonaro

, a hashtag #PesquiseOCasoAnaClara se tornou um mantra nas redes sociais. Motivo: Flávio é o advogado que manteve o policial Bruno Dias Delaroli, réu pelo assassinato da criança, fora da prisão até agora, como o presidente Lula lembrou no debate.


A história de Ana Clara ganhou repercussão nacional nas últimas semanas, depois que a série jornalística Revelando, criada pela equipe do videocast Calma Urgente, lançou um

episódio

 de 22 minutos sobre o caso, apresentado pela atriz Camila Pitanga. Em 2024, já senador da República, Flávio assumiu a defesa do PM e assinou um recurso apresentado ao Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) para tentar reverter a decisão que determinou o júri popular. Embora o pedido tenha sido negado, até hoje não houve julgamento.


Cristiane, a mãe da garotinha, recebeu muito apoio nas redes sociais, mas também sofreu ataques de apoiadores de Flávio e começou a se sentir ameaçada na região onde vive, no Largo da Batalha, Niterói, perto de onde sua filha foi morta. Tomada por uma crise de pânico e depressão, afastou-se das redes, e ainda foi despejada da casa onde vivia de favor, pois o dono é bolsonarista.


Ela viu trecho do debate entre Lula e Flávio: foi “desesperador ver que Flávio não respondeu a pergunta sobre Ana Clara”, diz. Para ela, “as pessoas não enxergam que sou uma mãe que perdeu uma filha, acham que quero prejudicar o Flávio, há quem diga que a errada fui eu por deixar meus filhos na porta de casa. Flávio defendeu e conseguiu anular o júri do cara, tentou fazer o cara não ser julgado pelo crime que cometeu. Tenho certeza que, se ele for eleito, o caso vai ser esquecido e eu nunca terei o descanso de saber que o assassino da minha filha está pagando pelo que ele fez.”


Cristiane não é uma militante de esquerda – no primeiro turno, ela nem votou, pois sua advogada achou melhor ela não sair de casa por causa das ameaças. Há cinco anos e seis meses aguarda o julgamento do assassino de sua filha ser marcado. A princípio seria em 14 de abril deste ano, dia em que Ana Clara completaria 11 anos de idade, mas foi adiado para 21 de outubro. No fim de agosto, o julgamento foi reagendado para 5 de maio de 2027. “Disseram que foi adiado novamente porque a juíza terá outro compromisso no dia. Só tem ela de juíza? E precisava jogar para o meio do ano que vem?”, revolta-se Cristiane. “A gente sabe que foi aquele policial, a perícia foi feita, a balística das armas foi feita, todos sabem que aquele homem foi o único que atirou, o delegado sabe disso, eu sei, o policial sabe. Mas estou à mercê da Justiça.”


Depois que Ana Clara morreu, a família se desestruturou. Seu caçula, Pedro, hoje com oito anos, ainda lembra da irmã que morreu ao seu lado. Ele faz tratamento com psicólogo desde então e não está morando com a mãe. “Ainda tenho a guarda, mas deixei ele com a avó. Não quero que ele passe pelo que estou passando. Meu sonho é conseguir um emprego para ter a minha casa e trazer ele de volta. Tenho medo que ele sinta que eu o abandonei”, lamenta a mãe.


Cristiane fala sobre como é difícil conseguir trabalho. Ela parou de estudar adolescente, quando engravidou da filha. “Eu tento, mando currículos pra tudo que é canto, faço faxina, mas não consigo nada certo. Preciso me fazer de forte todos os dias, mas às vezes não dá, a realidade da situação chega e bate pânico. Às vezes entrego os pontos e não quero ver ninguém, penso que já deu pra mim essa vida, mas então vejo o Pedro e quero ter ele comigo, preciso dele e ele também …

author: Darío Aranda
title: La nueva política contra el hambre se cocina en los comedores populares
content:
Por Leonardo Rossi*


Tal vez un síntoma clave de la degradación social que atravesamos sea la profunda aceleración de

la indolencia respecto al hambre

 de las otras y otros convivientes de esta Tierra que habitamos. Si bien no se trata de un fenómeno nuevo, sí emergen rasgos diferenciales en esta etapa, con la

violenta narrativa aplicada desde arriba por el gobierno de Javier Milei

 y con amplias porciones de la sociedad y sus subjetividades impermeables a la problemática. 


Se trata de enormes segmentos que exceden largamente al activismo libertariano. No obstante, en estas líneas se apunta a la contraparte de este escenario:

las organizaciones que les hacen frente y sí se hacen cargo del hambre del prójimo

. A las estrategias desde las que estas organizaciones enfrentan el actual escenario de violencias múltiples y sus deseos políticos —  “horizontes interiores”, como les llama

Raquel Gutiérrez Aguilar

—, que anidan alrededor de las ollas comunitarias.


En las últimas décadas, la situación del hambre en la Argentina fue abordada desde diversas políticas en clave asistencial como normalidad y no como paso a un abordaje de fondo. Los picos catastróficos de carencia alimentaria con geografías y segmentos sociales marcadamente diferenciados han sido profusamente analizados en investigaciones académicas, de ONGs, instituciones religiosas y movimientos sociales como el informe

“Rascar la olla”

 —Fundación Rosa Luxemburgo y CELS— o los trabajos del

Observatorio de la Deuda Social

, por mencionar algunos.


Si hubo una novedad con el actual Gobierno dentro del panorama de las últimas décadas fue la reivindicación discursiva de la producción política del hambre dentro de las reglas capitalistas y la efectiva concreción de ataques directos a las redes organizativas que soportan la alimentación de sus comunidades en condiciones de extrema precariedad económica.


Por eso, es necesario poner el foco en la potencia política que habita en los comedores barriales, a pesar de los múltiples desafíos existentes, e indagar qué nuevos imaginarios y prácticas se pueden abrir tirando del hilo que convidan las cocineras comunitarias para pensar en abordar el hambre a profundidad y cultivar redes agroalimentarias que logren trascender los cíclicos vaivenes de la macropolítica.


Foto: Plaga Colectiva


Las ollas encendidas, moral feminista-comunitaria


La tarea de las mujeres (abrumadora mayoría) que encabezan los comedores son harto complejas y diversificadas. Si con justa razón tantas veces se apunta a que las docentes deben abarcar trabajos que exceden largamente su rol específico, en el caso de las cocineras se trata de trabajadoras que, muy lejos de abocarse con exclusividad a la cocción de ingredientes, deben gestionar en términos muy concretos la creciente y angustiosa demanda por raciones, caminar horas recolectando retazos de madera de la calle e inventando con qué mantener el fuego encendido bajo las ollas frente a inexistentes garrafas, pedir donaciones —a veces a ocultas porque expone la deficitaria tarea de funcionarios locales, que toman represalias—. También hacer las veces de confidentes y asesorar ante crudos relatos de violencia de género, organizar festejos de cumpleaños que pueden ser únicos para muchas niñas y niños, y sigue la lista.


Si bien suele marcarse que la situación del hambre en el país no ha estallado debido al sostenimiento por parte del gobierno nacional de algunas políticas asistenciales a niveles inflacionarios o por encima de estos, menos se dice de la intensa tarea de estas mujeres a lo largo y ancho de la Argentina. Verdaderas artesanas que sostienen, recrean y buscan potenciar lo que resta de comunidad allí donde todo conspira para su horadación.


Si por apenas algunos días, se decretara una “huelga de ollas apagadas”  —recuperando el proceso de lucha encabezado por mujeres durante la primera mitad del siglo XX en Chile para enfrentar a empresas mineras— de todas las cocineras de comedores populares de Argentina, la situación social de seguro sentiría su cimbronazo. Una acción de protesta en esa clave no es concebible ni deseable, más se quiere trazar aquí una imagen que dimensione la relevancia de este trabajo vital que nace de lo profundamente comunitario en cada barrio y paraje del país. Imaginar de qué modo esos más de treinta mil espacios pudieran, cual una gran olla comunal, traducir su relevancia política y perturbar de modo efectivo la normalidad del poder …

author: Anikibawal
title: Comunicado de los PPM del Módulo comuneros de la Cárcel de Temuco tras el llamado a Marcha por la Resistencia, el 12 de octubre pasado.
content:
Comunicado de los presos políticos Mapuche del Módulo Comuneros de la Cárcel de Temuco tras el llamado a movilización Marcha por la resistencia, del pasado lunes 12 de octubre.


«Nosotros los prisioneros políticos mapuche recluidos en la cárcel de temuko saludamos a nuestras autoridades tradicionales y a todos quienes fueron participe de la gran movilización llevada adelante, el lunes 12 de octubre en la ciudad de temuko.


Mediante este escrito, venimos a agradecer la gran convocatoria realizada este 12 de octubre en apoyo concreto a los PPM de la cárcel de Temuco y a sus demandas, por parte del movimiento social en toda su amplitud.


Agradecemos a todos aquellos y aquellas que pusieron sus ganas y newen para que todo resultara de la mejor manera: a nuestros familiares, pu afkadi, autoridades tradicionales, comunidades en resistencia de diversos puntos del wallmapu, wenuy y simpatizantes de nuestra causa.


Hoy, a días de la gran movilización, creemos que esta logró los objetivos esperados con creces. Por tanto, agradecemos a nuestro pueblo por demostrar su fuerza cuando se lo propone.


La unidad en el weichan la entendemos como aquella en la que todo nuestro pueblo tiene su espacio, en sus distintas formas, con sus aciertos y errores. Aquí tienen cabida todos quienes busquen ser partícipes de la unidad que, como pueblo mapuche, merecemos darnos. Desde el pichiche hasta los kuifiche, todo nuestro pueblo tiene su espacio cuando se trata de levantar un movimiento social mapuche sólido, capaz de reunir la fuerza necesaria para luchar por lo que nos pertenece.


Eso sí, esta unidad debe construirse siempre desde la transparencia y la honestidad, sin dar cabida a los personalismos ni a las supuestas cualidades morales particulares.


Reconocemos también a cada uno de los peñi, ka pu lamngen y wenny de la causa mapuche que destinaron un día que podrían haber utilizado para descansar o compartir con sus familias en casa, y que, en cambio, se dieron el ánimo de asistir para expresar su solidaridad consciente con los familiares y los PPM.


Extendemos, finalmente, nuestros agradecimientos a todo el movimiento social mapuche que, cuando se lo propone, demuestra que es posible confluir en ideas y aspiraciones que aglutinan y suman. Esto cobra especial relevancia en los tiempos que corren, en los que la atomización y el individualismo prevalecen por sobre la justa intención de juntarse y organizarse, con el propósito de ser partícipes concretos del movimiento social mapuche autónomo.


Fei taiñ feipiaiñ may. Chaltu may kom eimun!¡¡KIÑEWKULEAIÑ WEICHAN MEW!!


Fin a las altas condenas


Fin a la dispersión de los PPM.


Fin al estado de excepción en Wall Mapu.


No a la aplicación de la ley Antiterrorista.


A más de 500 años de resistencia no pudieron ni podrán borrar la memoria del mapuzungun. «


*Enviado a la radio.


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

.

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

author: Comunizar
title: Revista Crítica Anticapitalista 6 – La Comuna, la clase y la lucha de clases
content:
PRESENTACION


¿Qué relación existe entre la Comuna como forma política de la emancipación social y la clase, entendida ésta no como categoría positivizada y sociológica, sino en su carácter dual y contradictorio? ¿Es la Comuna una manera de entender la clase y la lucha de clases en clave no identitaria, no positivizada? ¿La oposición entre Comuna y clase es algo derivado de una concepción anti-dialéctica de la lucha de clases? En ese campo ¿a qué dialéctica nos referimos? ¿A la dialéctica hegeliana orientada a la síntesis estatal como forma política de la identidad? ¿A la dialéctica negativa que la cuestiona? ¿La lucha de clases, entendida en clave dialéctica no-identitaria, permite entender la Comuna como proceso contradictorio de disolución de la clase? ¿Implica esto un desafío a nuestro concepto de proletariado y a la idea de revolución calcada en el canon leninista?


CONTENIDO


Comuna y Lucha de Clases


La Comuna y la lucha de clases hoy

 – Sergio Tischler


El Amanecer le gana a la Noche

 – John Holloway


La Comuna como la lucha de clases más profunda

 – Alejandro Olmo

– Gianluca Carmosino

Raoul Vaneigem, una toma de partido por la vida contra la sobrevivencia impuesta

 – Sagrario da Saúde


Sobre la Comuna

 – Raoul Vaneigem, Guy Debord y Attila Kotányi


Por la Comuna

 – La Comuna, Raoul Vaneigem


Seminario Comuna contra Estado


Comuna y Estado: experiencias de resistencia colectiva en Kurdistán y México

 – Diego Laurentis Sellers y Amara Öcalan


La forma-Estado y la Comuna: en antagonismo en su esencia

 – Áquilas Mendes


Pueblos indígenas, mujeres y lucha antiidentitaria

– Wendi Elizabeth Carrillo Isiordia


La Comuna como forma de vida

 – Francesca Randazzo Eisseman

 – Carlos Gabriel Huerta Recillas


La práctica comunizante de ollas comunes en América Latina y el Caribe

 – Lucía Dias da Silva Guerra

 – Leonardo Carnut

– Franco J. Quiroga

title: «No es aumento, es ajuste»: docentes bonaerenses rechazan el 6% de aumento de Kicillof y convocan a paros, ollas populares y movilizaciones
content:
Imagen: Política Obrera.


Las seccionales y agrupaciones de SUTEBA Multicolor y la Asociación de Maestrxs de la Provincia de Buenos Aires convocaron a nuevas medidas de fuerza contra el acuerdo salarial del 6%, en dos tramos del 3%, correspondientes a octubre y noviembre, acordado por la mayoría de los gremios que integran el Frente de Unidad Docente Bonaerense (FUDB) con el gobierno de Axel Kicillof. Las medidas incluyen un paro provincial para este martes 20 de octubre, otro para el miércoles 21, una olla popular frente a la Gobernación bonaerense y una movilización a la Dirección General de Cultura y Educación (DGCyE) para el próximo jueves 22.

La Multicolor denuncia que la conducción provincial de SUTEBA pretende aprobar la propuesta «sin mandato de las escuelas», reclama asambleas por establecimiento para definir las medidas de lucha y, además, la devolución de los descuentos por paros, la defensa del estatuto docente, el rechazo al presentismo, y mejoras en IOMA y en las condiciones de trabajo. En tanto, la Asociación de Maestrxs expresó:  «rechazamos por miserable la propuesta de aumento que le da la espalda a las necesidades de la docencia bonaerense. $10.491 al básico, $ 4.256 al código 455 en gris y $921 al incentivo docente en negro no es aumento, es ajuste».
