title: ¿Adiós “fenómeno barrial”? La ultraderecha internacional se despega de Milei
content:
En su visita a España, el Presidente no será recibido por el Gobierno ni los candidatos -tampoco “su amigo”, Santiago Abascal- y apenas mantendrá un “encuentro privado” con Díaz Ayuso. En Brasil, el propio Bolsonaro busca despegarse de la mala performance de su aliado argentino.


El espejismo de un Javier Milei aclamado por los foros internacionales, sobre todo ultraderechistas, definitivamente entró en crisis: tras casi dos años y medio de sobreexposición y protagonismo en cumbres conservadoras, el hombre de la motosierra experimenta un destrato que, incluso, alcanza a sus aliados geopolíticos.


Las cifras económicas y su consecuente reflejo en las encuestas, vuelve razonable el declive: un reciente estudio realizado por la Universidad de San Andrés reveló que el 67% de las personas consultadas rechaza “la marcha general” del país.


 | Lula a Bolsonaro durante el debate presidencial: “No tienes idea, anda a leer. Para que nunca vuelvas a decir que seguirás a Milei, ¿Ya le pediste prestada la motosierra?”. https://t.co/zvKjvN5vlw


— Alerta News 24 (@AlertaNews24)

October 19, 2026


En Brasil nadie quiere mirarse en ese espejo


En el escenario sudamericano, la experiencia argentina se convirtió en un insumo central de la campaña política en Brasil. El Partido de los Trabajadores (PT) desplegó una contundente contraofensiva en redes sociales que expone el deterioro social, el desplome del poder adquisitivo y el incremento del desempleo al sur del continente bajo el plan del Ejecutivo argentino.


La campaña es tan simple como devastadora para el relato oficialista: votar a Flavio Bolsonaro es elegir el modelo Milei y sus consecuencias.


Durante el reciente debate televisivo, el presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva utilizó la figura de la “motosierra” para acorralar a Flavio Bolsonaro. Lula forzó al referente conservador a definir si aplicará en Brasil un recorte de partidas presupuestarias similar al implementado en Argentina. La respuesta evasiva del hijo del expresidente puso en evidencia el temor a que la adhesión explícita al modelo mileísta condicione sus aspiraciones electorales.


En España nadie quiere esa foto


Por estos días, el Presidente visitará Madrid, una ciudad atravesada por la campaña electoral que en noviembre decidirá si Pedro Sánchez debe abandonar La Moncloa, y quién lo sustituirá. Ni Santiago Abascal (VOX) —pese a la cercanía histórica— ni Alberto Núñez Feijóo (Partido Popular), candidatos ultraderechistas y derechistas, recibirán a Milei.


El único contacto formal se limitó a un encuentro de carácter privado con la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso.


Analistas políticos españoles coinciden en que un apretón de manos con el jefe de Estado argentino representa hoy un riesgo electoral directo, en momentos donde la opinión pública europea observa con desconfianza el ajuste social.


Esta pérdida de influencia ya había quedado plasmada en su reciente visita a Nueva York y la negativa de Donald Trump recibirlo, y ni siquiera ofrendarle la habitual fotografía informal de pasillo. En un viaje inmediatamente posterior, esta vez a Europa, tampoco logró audiencias de peso con antiguos socios derechistas (por ejemplo, la primera ministra italiana, Giorgia Meloni).


El desgaste interno y la proyección exterior


Responde a una marcada erosión del capital político en el plano doméstico, donde la aprobación de la gestión oficial cayó a alrededor del 30% y la desaprobación superó el 60%, según la gran mayoría de encuestas.


El aura de invencibilidad y el concepto de “fenómeno barrial global” que sus seguidores dinamizaban en plataformas digitales chocan hoy contra los números de la economía real.


Según el mencionado estudio de Universidad de San Andrés, el 54% de los encuestados aseguró que los ingresos de su hogar no alcanzan y, dentro de ese grupo, el 35% respondió que tuvo que usar ahorros o recortar gastos y el 19% señaló que debió endeudarse.


Todo indica que hoy la ultraderecha internacional, atenta a las encuestas locales, prefiere tomar distancia antes de que la motosierra caiga sobre su intención de voto.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Philippines now in worst hunger crisis in 3 decades
content:
More Filipinos are experiencing hunger and even more admitted to being poorer in the third quarter of the year, a national survey reveals. Nearly a quarter of Filipinos said they experienced “being hungry and having nothing to eat at least once in the past three months.”


In a study conducted from September 21 to 27, survey firm Social Weather Station (SWS) said that 22.6 per cent of respondent families admitted to experiencing involuntary hunger, up by 2.3 points from 20.3 per cent in June.


It was the worse hunger rate in the country since 1998. This year’s hunger incidence is worse by 1.5 points above the record-high 21.1 per cent average of 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic


Where in the Philippines is hunger worse?


Hunger is worse in the capital region of Metro Manila at 27 per cent, the survey said, followed by Mindanao at 23.7 per cent.


Poverty is as bad in the rest of Luzon at 23.6 per cent while the Visayas region has fallen to 16.0 per cent.


This translates to an estimated 16.8 million Filipino families considered themselves poor in September, up from 13.6 million in June.


The September 2026 survey also found that 55 per cent of Filipino families rated themselves as “poor” while 9 per cent rated themselves as “borderline poor”


What does it mean to be poor in the Philippines?


SWS’ latest survey said 44 per cent of Filipinos rate themselves as “food poor,” eating simpler meals and less.


Food vendor Ramil said his customers had been buying his rice porridge less and less. He noticed that some of his customers who used to order twice a day now only eat once.


“Maybe because I had to increase my price by P5 per order,” he said, citing that cooking gas had increased by as much as 44 per cent since the war in the Middle East started early this year.


Ramil had also announced he is no longer giving credit to his customers. He sells at P50 per bowl.


In a nearby eatery, a basic dish with three small meat slices also increased to P80 while a small cup of rice sells at P20. “We give our customers extra spoonfuls of sauce to make it appear our servings have not shrunk. But everyone in this neighborhood knows the situation,” food vendor Joanna said.


Who’s to blame?


The SWS survey was conducted as the Philippines suffered its worst inflation rate for the second time since the start of the US-Israel war against Iran early in the year. Both April and September registered an alarming 7.2 per cent rate of increase in prices of goods and services.


Independent economic think tank Ibon Foundation squarely blamed the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. government’s “inaction” on inflation.


“The government is not using its national energy emergency powers to control domestic oil prices or to cap prices of basic goods, contended with giving dole outs to select groups,” Ibon executive director Sonny Africa said.


Africa said he hopes Marcos was informed of the September inflation rates last weekend, only to distract the Philippine president from fully enjoying the F1 Singapore Grand prix. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

title: Continued Arrests and State Repression in Tijmali Forests in Odisha
content:
Even as Adivasi and Dalit communities in Odisha’s Sijimali region continue to resist mining operations, the state has responded not with dialogue but with an intensifying crackdown on villagers aimed at breaking a sustained people’s movement against the bauxite project of Vedanta Limited in Kashipur block of Raygada district. The arrests of anti-mining solidarity struggle activists Dr. Randall Sequeira and Laxman Naik on October 16 on cooked up charges is part of the ceaseless violence and arbitrary arrests unleashed by the state government and mining corporate nexus since mid-2023.


 


October 18, 2026

: The ongoing state repression of the Adivasi and Dalit communities in South Odisha fighting to protect their land, forest and water resources including their hills, streams and their very identity, along with anti-mining activists supporting the people’s movements continues with the arrests of Dr. Randall Sequeira and Laxman Naik from Bhawanipatna, Kalahandi on the night of 16th October 2026.


 


Laxman Naik is a leading Dalit activist of the Ma Mati Mali Surakhya Manch, and also of Samajwadi Jan Parishad. Dr Randall Sequeria has been working with Adivasi communities in Kalahandi and Rayagada districts. Both are dedicated to supporting people’s movements in Odisha against dispossession and distress caused by mining and industrialization and in protecting human habitats.


 


They were detained for the entire night at Town Police station without providing them any access to their lawyers or family members. Both were produced in front of the SDJM, Rayagada in connection with Kashipur Police Station Case no. 85/2026, which is related to the

incidents

 that occurred in the intervening night of April 6th-7th in Kantamal Village, Rayagada, where a large police contingent entered into the village, leading to indiscriminate lathi-charge and firing of tear gas shells resulting in the injury of numerous villagers and police personnel.


 


Neither Laxman Naik’s nor Dr. Randall’s names are mentioned in the FIR. The Kashipur police has unleashed a battery of charges against the two ranging from attempt to murder, rioting armed with a deadly weapon, and criminal intimidation by threatening to cause death or grievous hurt.


 


Both of them have been subsequently sent to remand at the Rayagada Sub Jail.


 


The Concerned Citizens Committee, Odisha, has released a statement appealing to all democratic and progressive organizations, movements and individuals to express solidarity and demand the withdrawal of all criminal cases foisted on the struggling people of Odisha for Jal, Jangal and Jameen.


 


The full statement is published here.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Animal Rights Advocates Call for Referendum on Snare Traps
content:
ANIMAL RIGHTS ADVOCATES are currently campaigning for a referendum to be held on the use of wild boar snares.

In particular, animal rights advocates have long criticized wild boar snares as overly cruel. Such traps use spring-loaded mechanisms to tighten around animals’ limbs when triggered.

Nevertheless, such traps have also been criticized for ensnaring other species, as they do not distinguish. Endangered species such as Formosan black bears and leopard cats had also been killed by such traps, as have cats and dogs, sometimes resulting in their losing limbs if they survive.

Though claims had been made that Indigenous hunters used such traps as part of traditional hunting rights, animal rights groups have generally cited that this was rarely the case, in that Indigenous hunters generally do not use such traps. By contrast, such animal rights advocates state that Indigenous hunters more commonly use traps made from wood, bamboo and vines, and other natural materials. In the past, the Central Election Commission turned down calls for a referendum on the use of wild boar snares on the basis that the referendum was unclear as to whether it pertained to traps used by Indigenous hunters.

Otherwise, such traps are sometimes used by farmers as a means of preventing damage to their crops. Animal rights advocates have called on the government to provide electric fencing, protective netting, or other means for farmers to protect their livestock and crops.

The proposals called for by animal rights advocates are relevant to the use, display, and sale of wild boar snares, as well as their import and export. It is thought that China is a major source of some of the wild boar snares used in Taiwan.

It is unclear as to whether the Central Election Commission will approve the referendum currently called for by animal rights advocates. At the same time, without a major political party endorsing it as an issue, such a referendum is unlikely to gain traction. It is to be seen if either the DPP or KMT, or perhaps even both parties, throw their weight behind the proposal.

One notes that there have been cases of political bipartisanship between both major parties on the issue of animal rights in past years, as seen with politicians of both parties supporting enshrining animal rights in the constitution. Even so, such politicians ultimately did not prove serious about such promises outside of election campaigning, as a result of which neither the KMT nor DPP acted on claims in past election cycles that animal rights would see constitutional protection.

author: rti_admin
title: The IITs: Tragic Failures That Beget More Tragedies
content:
From a social perspective, the IITs are tragic failures that beget more tragedies.

But you already know the IITs are the pinnacle of Indian aspirations, achievements, accolades, blah-di-blah, right? How about we celebrate by taking a closer look at the graduates, the faculty, and the institution?

The institutional charter, briefly. The IITs were conceived in 1946 to support the country’s industrial development and help meet the nation’s technological challenges. Parliament’s 1961 Act declares them institutions of national importance. It charges them with instruction and research, and with the advancement of learning and dissemination of knowledge. The same Act says every institute shall be open to persons of either sex and of whatever race, creed, caste or class, in admitting or appointing students and teachers alike. [1] Later laws reserve seats for SC, ST and OBC students, PhD seats included, and, since 2019, teaching posts at every rank.

Start with the product. As any IIT alum would confirm, a majority of IIT graduates wouldn’t be able to properly describe what ‘engineering’ is. Poorly educated and narrowly conditioned to chase status from a young age, most of them used to end up in finance or as middle management in US IT firms, but have lately diversified into mercenary ouroboros via IIT coaching and YouTube influencing. The institute’s own numbers: in IIT Bombay’s placement report for 2023–24, 29% of offers were in engineering and technology. The rest went to IT, consulting, finance, analytics and “other”. [2]

The defence is usually the famous founders. Let’s do the math. Seats went from about 2k a year in the 80s to about 20k now, so total grads ~400k. Unicorn founders ~117, high value startup founders maybe four thousand if you’re generous. So, 0.03% and 1%. [3, 4] Like unicorns, these founders are statistical anomalies. Sensible folks within the system will themselves readily acknowledge that their success is mostly despite it rather than because of it. And given the stated mission, funnelling billions in public subsidy into private equity accumulation for a minuscule minority is cause for shame rather than something to tom-tom about.

This is the deal then. Ruin your childhood to join an exclusive band of svayambhu achievers. Concoct jagatguru-brand gig economy “innovations” for exploiting cheap labor. Garland each other for contributions to the economic miracle of jobless growth and extractive digital feudalism. Parade your arrogant indifference or offer defensive apologies for the mockery of a social contract, dressed up in a lazy pragmatism argument about success.

By the way, who’s even there to teach them? Across all 23 IITs, 4,804 of 12,498 sanctioned teaching posts stood vacant in January 2026, or 38.4%. [5] It was 38.3% in December 2022. [6] In the nine IITs that disclosed the breakdown, about 60% of the empty posts were reserved ones. [5] Cryogenic sthiratva.

Sour grapes? I was there, eating them for four lost years. So chill. First week in the hostel, the rank was a common icebreaker question you asked people along with where they were from and in what department. Some hesitant answers made me stop asking. Only the rare, confident stud would openly declare he was SC, came through the preparatory course etc. The term in use was ‘schaddu’, and people would murmur in the early semesters, but soon some of them were ahead on GPA, and the murmurs lost voice. Years later, a friend who got a PhD mentioned feeling conflicted using reservations since their father was also a PhD and they went to good schools. Not long ago, an alum stated that even though they got in via reservation, everything after was earned by merit. I couldn’t make out if this was being defensive or proud. I don’t remember hearing of any campus suicides, and only learned about them from ‘The Death of Merit’ documentary. [7]

A decade after graduation and on another continent, the sourness still stung, in an interview by another pitiable alum. I was struggling for purpose and careening across career lanes. Unusual for an IIT grad, and he got suspicious… maybe I was a ‘category candidate’? So he asked for my rank, and then I asked for his, and then he said that’s not relevant, and then I agreed, and the interview went downhill. So, no chill.

Then the people who run the place. Do the IITs still hire blatantly sexist dogs as professors? It used to be de rigueur in several departments. A lot of the students were of a similar breed …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: On liberal opportunism and the “purity” smear
content:
Photo from Naga City Tourism Facebook page

Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic.

Why did former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo roll out the pink carpet for the Zionist war machine? When Robredo hosted Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh for an official courtesy visit, she was not merely performing the routine gestures of local hospitality. She was actively welcoming and legitimizing representatives of the US-Israeli genocidal apparatus. This intervention centers an anti-imperialist analysis to dismantle the liberal apologetics surrounding this act. Rather than an isolated error in judgment, this diplomatic encounter exposes the persistent, foundational tension within the Philippine political landscape: the contradiction between liberal reformism and anti-imperialist national liberation.

Dismissing progressives’ critique of Robredo’s hosting of the Israeli envoy as mere “political purism” is politically and morally impoverished. The underlying mechanism demands a total, systematic critique. To understand why her defenders deploy the “politics of purity” accusation, and why that defense completely falls apart when examining real power dynamics and economic interests, we must lay bare both the liberal class position and the ideological sleight of hand at work.

To make sense of Robredo’s pivot toward imperial hospitality, we must look directly at the liberal class position. Her stance is neither an accidental misstep nor a personal failure of political intelligence but the direct expression of her class character and political alignment. Liberal reformism in the global periphery operates strictly within the legal, institutional, and geopolitical framework dictated by US imperialism.

While Robredo served as a focal point against the overt state terrorism of the Marcos-Duterte dynasties, her opposition was strictly intra-class—a feud over how to manage the neocolonial state, pitting rule-of-law decorum against autocratic violence.

Because her political legitimacy rests upon acceptance by the global capitalist order, her opposition stops at the border of imperial interest. When forced to choose between international solidarity with an anti-imperialist national liberation movement and alignment with the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, liberal reformists invariably side with the imperial core. They cannot critique the drain of value, the extraction of labor, or the military hegemony of US imperialism because their entire political project depends on remaining within that very apparatus.

This structural subservience explains why defenders deploy the “purity politics” weapon whenever that alignment is exposed. Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic. From a materialist standpoint, this argument relies on three ideological fallacies:

First, it replaces a materialist baseline with ideological absolution. Opposition to active genocide, ethnic cleansing, and imperialist aggression is not a performative or elevated ideological standard; it is the absolute baseline of human solidarity and anti-imperialist struggle. Labeling principled opposition to mass slaughter as “purity” redefines baseline morality as an unreasonable demand, attempting to pass off complicity as pragmatic maturity.

Second, it operates on the logic of liberal idealism, which treats political stances as abstract moral choices made in a vacuum. Political actions reflect concrete class interests. Shielding a public figure from accountability for legitimizing a settler-colonial state serves a specific political function: it conditions the middle forces to accept imperial violence as a routine, acceptable feature of global diplomacy.

Third, it trades scientific alignment for unprincipled unity. Transformative praxis distinguishes between principled unity—built on anti-imperialist struggle and mass interest—and unprincipled unity, which colludes with reaction to preserve electoral coalitions. Demanding that the progressive movement remain silent on international solidarity to protect a liberal politician’s image trades human rights and anti-imperialist consciousness for temporary electoral expediency.

title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.

content:
with added reports from Jessica Obciana and Kline Vergara

“Homes are destroyed, livelihoods are lost, nations are lost by interests that are made far beyond our own borders. Even now, initiatives like Pax Silica, supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors are being reordered around the needs of the US war machine, and countries like us [the Philippines] are being asked to serve as suppliers and now become their targets, rather than being allowed to decide our own development,” said Dr. Giovanni Tapang, convener of the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Network.

Various anti-imperialist groups gathered for the webinar Updates from the Resistance: The Current Situation in Iran, Palestine, Venezuela, and Cuba, co-organized by BAYAN, the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Campaign Network, to express people’s solidarity in lambasting US imperialism following its sanctions, blockades, military aggression, and other forms of intervention and coercion against the people.

“We have seen the case of Venezuela: how this warfare has been attacking the Global South, attacking the country, and in many, many aspects, not only the political one, military, economic, and cultural, and in social consciousness. Venezuela is under siege now,” said Richard Lobo, Venezuela’s Chargé d’Affaires.

Venezuela possesses the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, estimated at around 303 billion barrels as of 2023, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Lobo noted that US intervention in Venezuela extends beyond economic sanctions to political, military, economic, and cultural intervention.

In January 2026, the US launched Operation Absolute Resolve as a large-scale military operation in Venezuela framed around drug trafficking and national security that led to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores and their transfer to the United States. Such an operation also targeted Venezuelan military infrastructure across Caracas and other locations.

Months after Maduro’s capture, the US laid out an agreement to gain access and control over an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil reserves, mineral wealth, and other resources.

Meanwhile, Lobo emphasized that the situation has only amplified the resistance among Venezuelans in defending their sovereignty and their right to determine the country’s political and economic direction.

“Even though we have been under attack […] the people there in Venezuela have been resisting and have been struggling. And one thing that I can say right now is that even with the kidnapping of our president, they believe the government is still in power,” Lobo stated.

title: Archaeological site believed to date back to the Abbasid period discovered in Babil
content:
The Press Office of Iraq’s Babil Governorate announced the discovery of an archaeological site in the Qasim district believed to date back to the Abbasid period, approximately 1,200 years ago.

According to a statement issued by the Press Office, the governor visited the site, examined the remains, assessed their historical significance, and discussed ways to preserve them.

The statement noted that the discovery could provide an opportunity to develop tourism in the district and promote its historical sites. It also highlighted the possibilities for developing the site as a tourist destination within the framework of laws governing the protection of existing archaeological heritage.

author: groundxero
title: Another One Bites the Dust: Construction Workers’ Not So Quiet Battle For Survival Ahead of Delhi’s Long Winter
content:
The ‘annual ban’ on construction work through the winter seasons in Delhi that has become tradition over the last half a decade due to an acute air pollution crisis in the city, has this year, become a starvation sentence.


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


15 October 2026, New Delhi:

 The rain falls in sheets on Thursday morning, ice cold and sudden like it can only get during mid-October weeks as Autumn bleeds into Winter. The wide, planned roads of Delhi’s Civil Lines region don’t flood quite so much as Shankar Road and its tributaries (or, god forbid, Gurgaon) but it’s enough to drench the lower halves of even the umbrella havers stuck underneath foot-over bridges and bus stops. 


 


Needless to say, the roads are abandoned. At the T-Point facing the DRDO office, a lone rickshaw puller stops abruptly, shivering as he holds the thin gamchha protecting his head tighter over him and runs to the shelter of the bridge. I stand there, too. Water has been steadily gathering at the top, and has now begun flooding down the stairs, soaking his sandalled feet and into my socks and shoes. When the rain slows, for a minute, I make to leave, aiming for the bus stop 50 metres away in case it starts up again.


 


The rickshaw puller warns me not to do that. I tell him I have somewhere to be. He asks me where I’m trying to go. I tell him there’s a protest today at Vikas Bhawan. 


 


“Look at the weather. No one’s protesting in the middle of this. Only a lunatic would be out there today.”


 


He is, of course, wrong. 


***


 


At Thursday noon, nearly 50 construction workers led a march from Vikas Bhawan to the Sushruta Trauma Centre, led by the AICCTU’s Building Workers’ Union, many of them travelling from faraway districts like Burari and Okhla. This was ahead of an announcement by the Delhi government that construction work in the city would be banned for a period of three months between November and January, ostensibly due to air pollution concerns, except the Supreme Court’s directions that such a blanket ban on work must be accompanied by the provision of minimum wages to aggrieved workers are not only nowhere close to being fulfilled, but are in fact being violated for a consecutive season since the Rekha Gupta led BJP came to power in 2025. 


 


“The Welfare board website has been down for nearly four months now,” said Ranjan Kuswaha, a mason and secretary of the local Burari unit of the Building Workers’ Union. “They said they were making a new one. And now that they have, they’ve already announced a seasonal ban less than two weeks away, beginning on November 1st and ending on January 31st. And till now this website is taking neither new registrations nor renewals. How on earth is the worker supposed to survive?”


 


Kushwaha further highlighted the plight of the migrant worker, so many of whom come to Delhi to work contractually on the many building and developmental projects undertaken here annually, who will now be left destitute. 


 


Advocate Surya Prakash Union said that a majority of the workers associated with the BWU hail from Supaul and Saharsa, two of Bihar’s poorest districts. 


“Most of our workers come from the poorest regions,” Surya Prakash, AICCTU; Infographic via BWU.


“We demand that this website be fixed at the earliest, and that registrations and renewals be completed as soon as possible and the workers be provided their labour cards,” Kuswaha said. 


 


There is also the matter of alleged gross corruption within this “welfare board” itself—the Delhi Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board (DBoCWWB), an organisation founded in 2002 in reference to the 1996 BoCW Act, which is apparently as much of a handful as it as a mouthful, according to the workers whose welfare it proclaims to oversee.


 


“On paper, the welfare framework for Delhi’s construction workers promises them wide-ranging support in almost all spheres of life: from maternity care, pension, housing, healthcare, education and even free daily commute on govt buses,” wrote Ishita Jairath for the Times of India in her scathing January 2026 report,

Hands That Build Delhi Brick By Brick Out Of Welfare Framework. 


 


The ground reality, however, was that the intended beneficiaries she asked about the schemes meant for them had nothing more than a “blank look”.


 


“Bitto, a marble and tile worker from Mangolpuri, didn’t know his children are eligible for education assistance,” Jairath wrote. “Preeti, a …

author: Brian Hioe
title: In A First, China Sanctions Ministers of Diplomatic Allies of Taiwan
content:
THE CHINESE GOVERNMENT has sanctioned two government ministers from diplomatic allies of Taiwan. These would be Belizean Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca and Paraguayan Minister of Information Gustavo Villate. Such sanctions prevent them and their family members from doing business in China.

China does not appear to have sanctioned ministers of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies in the past. This would be a new means, then, of pressuring countries to switch ties from Taiwan to China.

Taiwan is larger than all of its diplomatic allies, whether measured in terms of the size of population or economy. The main reason why Taiwan maintains ties with its diplomatic allies is so that they can speak up for it in international organizations in which Taiwan is not a member.

That being said, Taiwan has also long been accused of “dollar diplomacy”–paying off diplomatic allies through infrastructure investment deals or slush money to high-ranking politicians in return for recognition. Indeed, one notes that many of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies are countries that have questionable human rights records.

Though China offers much the same to such allies in return for switching recognition, Taiwan is unable to outspend China. China is, of course, much larger than Taiwan. Likewise, small states risk being shut ouf of the lucrative–and much larger–Chinese market if they retain ties with Taiwan.

At times, the question of whether to maintain ties with Taiwan or break them in favor of Taiwan is a dividing issue between the two major political parties of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies. Another question for such countries, however, is that of ties with the US. The US does not diplomatically recognize Taiwan either, but it has in the past sought to shore up Taiwan’s existing diplomatic allies, maintaining ties with it. Indeed, one notes that Taiwan’s existing diplomatic allies are often also closer to the US, rather than China, and this proves another means of the US extending its influence in Latin and Central America, or among Pacific states.

The Chinese government has sanctioned American government officials such as Marco Rubio in the past, over hawkish stances on China, criticism of China’s human rights record, and support for Hong Kong. It may not be surprising to see China targeting government officials of countries that express support for Taiwan, then. This would follow up on how sanctions on Taiwanese government officials may in themselves be ineffective, seeing as such individuals and their family members may already know better than to do business in China. But it is not impossible that some of those that China eventually targets do, in fact, have business holdings in China. As such, it is to be seen whether this proves an effective means of pressure on diplomatic allies of Taiwan.

author: Ash Phthalo
title: City of Sydney for Palestine joins calls for council to boycott Airbnb
content:
City of Sydney for Palestine is joining housing justice organisers to call on the City of Sydney Council to boycott Airbnb and support strong laws for short-stay rentals.

Airbnb is a target of the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement because of its role in enabling tourism in illegal Israeli settlements in the Occupied West Bank.

Airbnb helps normalise Israel’s occupation, apartheid and dispossession of Palestinians from their homeland by listing and profiting from accommodation on stolen Palestinian land.

Airbnb is helping turn occupied land into a tourism market. It is helping normalise dispossession. It is making money while Palestinians are denied freedom, safety and return.

Airbnb is also part of the housing crisis in Australia.

There is severe housing stress in the Sydney, where Rents are rising and vacancies are low. Meanwhile, thousands of homes are being used as short-term rentals through platforms like Airbnb.

Sydney’s vacancy rate was just 2.1%, according to the ABC in August, but there were 10,531 active Airbnb listings.

Airbnb and short-term rental platforms allow homes to be converted into commercial tourist accommodation, while renters are pushed further into crisis.

The Sydney Greens have been campaigning for investor Airbnbs to be banned in the City of Sydney. Community groups, including Australia Palestine Advocacy Network (APAN) are joining the campaign.

Right now, weak registration systems and a lack of transparency make it difficult for residents, councils and regulators to identify and stop unlawful short-term rental accommodation.

New York City’s Local Law 18, implemented in 2023, created a stronger registration and verification system for short-term rentals. Hosts must register. Platforms are prohibited from processing bookings for unregistered short-term rentals.

Whole homes cannot be rented out as short-term accommodation for less than 30 days. Short-term rentals are only permitted where the host is staying in the same home as the guests, maintains a common household with them, and hosts no more than two paying guests at a time.

New York’s Local Law 18 laws have been shown to be effective, driving down anti-social short-term rentals from 40,000 to 3,522 over three years. While it will not fix the housing crisis, it shows that registration, lawful-use checks, platform verification and platform liability can help.

The City of Sydney for Palestine is calling on City of Sydney Council to boycott Airbnb and adopt laws including: no whole-home short-term rentals under 30 days and restrictions on investor-owned and non-primary-residence short-term rentals in high-pressure housing areas.

It also wants the NSW Labor government to give councils stronger powers to regulate, restrict and enforce against unlawful short-term rental accommodation.

[Join the Boycott Airbnb; Palestine and housing solidarity action on November 16, 4:30pm, outside Sydney Town Hall ahead of the City of Sydney Council meeting. Sign the petition.]

author: Luca Tavan
title: How the Socialist Party is different from the other parties
content:
Members of the Socialist Party are often asked what makes us different from other parties. Prospective left-wing voters bruised by the long history of politicians selling out their principles want to know how we will avoid becoming part of the same establishment we want to challenge. On the other hand, some left-wing Greens question whether the Socialist Party is even necessary, seeing as their party already offers similar policies. 

The only way to answer these questions properly is to explain how the Socialist Party is unlike any other in Australian politics. We have a vision of society and a political strategy that differs fundamentally from all pro-capitalist parties, from the Liberals to the Greens. So what’s so distinctive about our project? 

Socialism!

The first thing is in the name. We are a socialist party, avowedly opposed to the whole capitalist system. Of course, the meaning of the term “socialism” is contested. Many progressive politicians, from UK Greens’ Zack Polanski to New York’s Zohran Mamdani, have ridden a wave of hostility toward right-wing billionaires and use the term “socialism” to describe their goal of reformed capitalism. 

But we don’t just want to tinker with the system: the Socialist Party wants to get rid of capitalism. We oppose an economy based on private business ownership and the exploitation of workers. We support a democratic, socialised economy that abolishes the profit motive and allocates labour and resources based on human need. So we fight the class of business owners and challenge the political and legal system that exists to defend their rule. We think the workers who make everything run, from the transport system to warehouses to our hospitals, should be in charge, not business owners and politicians. 

Our policies reflect this: they’re not just about explaining how the world could be made nicer. They express a fundamental hostility to the fact that our society is organised around profit-making. They’re an argument that the wealth of the rich and the assets of corporations are the products of their exploitation of workers, and that we want to take back as much of that wealth as we can. 

Parties can easily adopt socialist terminology, especially when it seems popular. But actually fighting for socialism is another matter. The Australian Labor Party, for instance, adopted the socialist objective into its constitution in 1921:

“The Australian Labor Party is a democratic socialist party and has the objective of the democratic socialisation of industry, production, distribution and exchange, to the extent necessary to eliminate exploitation and other anti-social features in these fields.”

This came at a time when demand for socialism was widespread in the workers’ movement. But party leaders never took the objective seriously. The qualification “to the extent that” was tacked on to signal to capitalists that the ALP didn’t really intend to turn the tables on the economic system. Despite remaining in the party constitution to this day, Labor has been utterly committed to defending the priorities of the capitalist class for over a century. 

For us, socialism is more than just a word—it is our core philosophy.

Building the workers’ movement

That gets to the second thing that makes us different: socialists have a completely distinct strategy for changing the world. Because we think workers should run things, everything we do is shaped by the goal of rebuilding the capacity of workers to organise, demand more, and take on their bosses. 

That’s why Socialist Party members played a crucial role in the Victorian teachers’ strikes earlier this year. Negotiations over pay, conditions and school funding provided an opportunity to organise more socialist teachers, argue for an uncompromising form of trade unionism that doesn’t just accept Labor’s crumbs, and prove in practice that strikes can win real gains. 

Rather than the movement existing to serve parliamentarians, Socialist Party MPs would be bound to use their positions to serve the movement. They would be forbidden from taking all the income that comes with a seat in parliament—they would have to give most of it back to the movement, rather than build their own wealth from their position. No other party is for this—their parliamentary leaders all get filthy rich.

Our inspirations include socialists like Broken Hill miners’ leader Percy Brookfield, who decided to run for NSW parliament while sitting in a prison cell for …

author: Sarah Webber, Sue Bolton, Jacob Andrewartha
title: Do we really need AI mega data centres?
content:
Sarah Webber, a lecturer at the School of Computing and Information Systems at the University of Melbourne, joined Green Left Radio’s Jacob Andrewartha and Sue Bolton on October 9 to discuss the government-corporate push for mega data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) and what a different approach would look like.

There has been a lot of discussion about AI data centres being critical infrastructure. Do we need these mega AI data centres and what is the difference between cloud data centres and AI data centres?

Let’s first focus first on large language models (LLMs), the type of model that underlines ChatGPT or Gemini. The main reason for this rapid AI facilities construction is the race between the United States tech companies and their need to hang on to their investors as they try and build out LLMs which is a new form of wealth extraction.

There is no meaningful race that Australia or Victoria can be part of.

Proponents say that the LLMs will drive greater economic productivity; they’ll “grow the pie”. But there will actually be very few jobs after construction.

I’ve been studying the specifics of how productivity from LLMs would benefit Australians and the answers are all worryingly vague; I cannot see the evidence that there will be societal benefits from these LLMs.

Even CSIRO experts say, at best, the evidence for greater productivity is mixed and any productivity that does come from them is going to involve giving more money to those overseas tech companies. That means less jobs here, and fewer contracts for local businesses, but more wealth for a few billionaires and more inequality.

Some people are not sure whether they should oppose or support mega AI data centres. Do we need mega AI data-centres and LLMs to be able do everything we want to do online?

No, not at all. We already have a fair number of data centres around Australia and overseas. We have other ways of getting the technology that we need day-to-day. If we want to pull back our data centres and reduce energy emissions in our information communication technologies, that’s totally feasible.

We can still watch television, send emails, store our personal photos online and have backups. We can do all that without new data centres. A lot of the capabilities that are being built are not for things that any of us are asking for.

There is a groundswell of grassroots opposition to the construction of these mega AI data centre, which has pushed the Victorian Labor government to make new rules around their construction and regulation. What do you make of these changes?

These new regulations are inadequate.

First up, the 150-metre buffer between the new data centres and homes is not far enough. Air-pollutants from diesel generators at data centres will affect people much further away than 150 metres.

Large AI data centres have massive fluctuations in energy demands and so when the power needs to spike, they fire up these massive diesel generators. That not only means pollution from burning diesel, but there is also a risk of fire from storing diesel on-site.

There is also noise, bright lighting, as well as the industrialisation and heat effects, all of which will affect people much further away than 150 metres.

More significantly, there is really no benefit for people living around it. AI data centres are not a necessary evil; we simply don’t need them.

In fact, we can imagine a dystopian scenario where the communities of people put out of work by AI are living right next to the data centres housing the AI systems.

The federal and state governments are making a big deal about forcing AI data centres to use renewable energy and to produce their own water. Can you comment on this?

The intention is to pay a local renewables provider to build additional capacity. But those companies already have loads of renewable projects in the pipeline so the most likely way these data centre companies are going to meet the requirement is to pay the renewables provider to put their name on an existing project. There won’t be any new energy supply.

author: Barry York
title: From student activism to Pentridge and beyond: the life of Barry York
content:
Barry York was a leading student radical at La Trobe University at the height of the movement against the Vietnam War. In 1972, along with two other student activists, Barry was arrested and held in Pentridge Prison for his anti-war activity. He recently self-published a memoir of his time in Pentridge as a political prisoner which will soon be available at Red Flag books.

The La Trobe struggle was part of the wider student movement opposing the Vietnam War, conscription and apartheid in the late 1960s and early 1970s. On campus, we challenged the university’s ties to political and economic power, including Chancellor Sir Archibald Glenn’s association with ICI (Imperial Chemical Industries, renamed Orica Limited in 1998), which had contracts with the government linked to the Vietnam War. ICI’s parent company also had links to the munitions and chemicals industries in apartheid South Africa. We opposed La Trobe’s rule barring students suspended elsewhere from enrolling, and questioned its possible cooperation with the Joint Intelligence Organisation. At the heart of these campaigns was a basic question: whose interests should a university serve?

At a mass student meeting in April 1971, attended by about 1,000 people, students endorsed demands for action on these issues. It must be noted that, at that time, La Trobe was a small campus and probably only had about 1,500 students on campus at any time. The campaign involved meetings, leafleting, debate, occupations and demonstrations. In July, students blockaded the university governing body, the Council, inside its chambers. The action had been endorsed at a student meeting, but it prompted a heavy police response and intensified the conflict between student activists and university authorities. Several activists were suspended and a larger number were fined. However, we won two key demands—the Chancellor’s resignation was announced in December, and the exclusion rule was rescinded.

This did not end the dispute though. The university authorities sought to stop the Student Representative Council from using its funds to pay the fines imposed on radical students who had been suspended. The fines totalled $3,000: a substantial amount, equivalent to about $40,000 today. Early the following year, the university sought a Supreme Court injunction barring four student activists from entering the campus. When we defied it, Fergus Robinson, Brian Pola and I were imprisoned for contempt of court. Rod Taylor evaded capture.

We were held indefinitely at Pentridge prison, a notorious high-security prison, without a criminal trial, the right to bail or appeal, or the opportunity to cross-examine witnesses. No fixed sentence was imposed. We would remain in prison until the university authorities asked the court to release us. The case raises lasting questions about freedom of expression, judicial power and the use of imprisonment to suppress political dissent.

That struggle forms the background to my memoir. Pentridge Prison closed in 1997, but the reality of life inside its bluestone walls should not be forgotten. The prison has been transformed into apartments, landscaped gardens, shops and fashionable cafés. Much of its brutality has been softened, repackaged or concealed by the redevelopment.

I wanted to recover that history by describing what it was like to be held at Pentridge as a political prisoner, first in D Division and then in A Division. Through observation and conversations with other prisoners, I also came to understand conditions in B and C Divisions and the notorious H Division, known as “Hell”.

The imprisonment of the “La Trobe Three” as we were called shows how fragile our freedoms can be. In writing the memoir, I also wanted to challenge the familiar, softened account of the youth rebellion of that era. The movement was about much more than sex, drugs, rock’n’roll and counterculture. Opposition to conscription, the Vietnam War and apartheid were central concerns. Many young people took their politics seriously; some sought revolutionary change as well as reform and were prepared to make personal sacrifices. Conventional accounts often leave that commitment in the background.

My political engagement with Pentridge continued after my release. From 1973 to 1976, I played a leading role in the Victorian Prisoners’ Action Committee. We campaigned against brutality and degrading conditions and brought prisoners’ experiences into public debate. We organised …

author: Maharnav Bhuyan
title: Why the far right’s favorite target is Indians
content:
A handful of men from the far-right National Workers Alliance yelled this at a rally for Indian democracy near Victorian Parliament on October 18. They chanted “Go back, go back” and held a blue banner stating “START REMIGRATION”, the right’s euphemism for mass deportation.

Police removed an uninvited speaker and moved the group aside.

The rally, backed by The Humanism Project and Hindus for Human Rights, answered with a chant of their own: “We welcome migrants.” The protest was called to support the youth-led protests that have filled India’s streets since early October, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign because the electoral rolls dropped more than 130 million names.

The Indian Express revealed in September that two of Kumar’s fellow commissioners had objected at least 14 times in 10 months, including to decisions allegedly made without their knowledge. The commission insists its revision decisions were unanimous.

Kumar was appointed under a 2023 law that removed the Chief Justice from the selection panel and handed the government two of its three seats. In April, the presiding officers of India's parliament refused to admit opposition notices, signed by 193 MPs, to remove him.

One placard in read: “They deleted my name, not my voice.”

Nativism is the idea that a nation belongs only to its “native” people. One Nation and India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) speak it fluently.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson told the National Press Club in June that Australia should be a “monocultural society”. Prime Minister Narendra Modi told a 2024 campaign rally that the opposition would hand people’s wealth to “infiltrators”, remarks widely condemned as an attack on Muslims. Hanson has twice worn a burqa prop into the Senate and was suspended last November for seven sitting days.

Both parties offer an anxious majority “civilisational” pride and an “enemy” within.

The anthropologist Arjun Appadurai named the engine beneath both, in 2006, as an “anxiety of incompleteness”, in which a majority turns on a small minority because it reminds it that its dream of a pure nation is unfinished.

Hindutva (the BJP’s Hindu nationalism) and Hansonism rise in different mountains and meet in the same muddy confluence. I call this mirror nativism: one grammar, two peoples, each able to see the other only as a threat.

That is why Australia’s far right has never warmed to Modi.

Before he addressed more than 20,000 people at Marvel Stadium on July 9, the far-right March for Australia promoted an anti-migration protest. Outside the stadium, a small far-right contingent protested Indian immigration and Modi himself.

Nearby, the Alliance Against Islamophobia protested his record on Muslims. One protest opposed what Modi does and the other opposed what he is.

It is often assumed that the far right hates Indians because there are so many of us.

The numbers say otherwise. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) in June last year counted 971,020 India-born residents — 3.5% of the population — and, for the first time on record, the largest overseas-born group.

Second came the English-born at 970,950. Seventy people separate the two communities. Nobody marches against the English!

The far-right’s favourite statistic fares no better. March for Australia flyers claimed: “More Indians in 5 years, than Greeks and Italians in 100”. AAP FactCheck found that net migration from Greece and Italy over the century was 517,883, almost double India’s largest-ever five-year figure of 279,450.

India supplied 48,326 of the 185,001 permanent migration places in 2024-25 and more new citizens than any other nationality over 2023-2024.

About 110,000 Indian students, or 16% of all international students, studied here in the first half of this yea. It is roughly one India-born resident in nine. We pay full fees and a $2000 visa charge. We keep university budgets afloat. We are told our rooms are why rents go up.

We cannot vote. But those who are citizens can, which is what alarms Liberal Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price, who told the ABC last year that “there is a concern with the Indian community”, citing its numbers and its Labor vote. She was removed from the opposition frontbench.

In Truganina, in Melbourne’s west, more than a quarter of residents were Indian-born at the 2021 Census.

Hated as transients and hated as voters makes us the convenient stranger. Sociologist Georg Simmel, in 1908, defined the stranger as one …

author: Robert Narai
title: France’s student revolt
content:
Video footage shows tens of thousands of school students packed into Place de la République in Paris, chanting, “High schools in struggle! Youth on fire! The revolution is on the march!” It’s 6 October, and outside Lamartine high school, students hold placards that read, “More class hours than sleep” and “8am to 6pm, are we students or in police custody?”

“We are protesting because we deserve the right to have a good life”, Lyna tells 

Red Flag

 via text from the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis. She is a 16-year-old 

lycéenne

 (high schooler aged 15 to 18) at Paul-Éluard; her parents are Algerian immigrants. Lyna says many young people like her have lost faith that school will lead anywhere. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s budget proposes €54 billion in public spending cuts and the abolition of 1,588 teaching posts. Combined with police who treat young people from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) like 

racaille

 (“scum”) and a growing far right, it has created a disaffected layer of young people.

“There are cockroaches and rats everywhere”, Lyna says of her classrooms. “We have classes that go from 8am to 6pm. The police harass us on the streets because of the colour of our skin and the 

banlieue

 we live in. We, the children of the 

banlieues

, are abandoned and neglected.” Yet students in better parts of Paris have joined Lyna. “We know we’re privileged, but we support the other 

lycées

”, a student at a private Catholic school told 

Public Sénat

 at the 6 October demonstration.

“

Lycéens

, and even 

collégiens

 [ages 11 to 15], are fighting above all against the two-tier education system they are victims of”, says Arthur, a student at Lycée Charlemagne in Paris and member of the New Anticapitalist Party–Revolutionaries (NPA-R), via message. “On one side, there is pressure at every level to ‘succeed at school’ or you have no future. But on the other, everyone can see that it’s cash that determines ‘success’. Year after year, the number of students per class keeps rising, up to 35, and students go weeks, even months, without a maths or French teacher.”

How the revolt unfolded

The revolt began on 21 September, when about 200 students at Saint-Exupéry high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, blockaded their school. Within days, the blockades spread across the Paris region, as students in poor and migrant suburbs linked their own conditions—including Parcoursup (an online platform that allocates places at public universities, which entrenches class and racial inequality)—to decades of funding cuts. Hundreds of thousands of students have since joined strikes and demonstrations against the government of Emmanuel Macron, and the revolt has moved beyond the demand for decent schools into a confrontation with austerity, police violence and racism. On 29 September, more than 300,000 people marched in a public sector strike against the budget, carrying signs reading “70 billion euros for the army, nothing for education”. By 1 October, the Interior Ministry reported actions at more than 1,000 schools.

In each blockaded school, daily mass meetings (“assemblies”) decide the next day’s action, and the disempowerment of ordinary life is turned on its head. Arthur says debating the questions the movement raises gives students ownership over it. “The government sought to break the movement by discrediting high school students as rioters ‘manipulated by La France Insoumise’ [France Unbowed, the left-wing party led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon]”, he says. 

“Some students target the police, and rightly so, which has sparked debate: how can the division sought by the government be avoided? What is certain is that in the assemblies we all agree not to be divided, to denounce police violence, to demand the release of all arrested students, and to say what the placards in Lyon say: ‘The burning of garbage only scares the garbage’.”

And as the revolt spreads to every kind of high school, Arthur asks, “How can we maintain the working-class character of the movement and its demands, which was its initial strength, without it dissolving into a kind of ‘everyone together’ mentality?”

National coordination has emerged across the assemblies: 200 delegates from 71 schools met on 10 October and called actions for 13, 15 and 17 October. “No way our struggle is going to be stolen by others!”, Arthur says.

State repression

The demonstrations have been met with fierce repression from the police. By 8 …

author: Ridah Hassan
title: Manosphere making classrooms toxic
content:
“I had male students threatening to rape the female students consistently. They would play ‘rape marry kill’ and used my own name frequently in their ‘game’.”

“Students saying ‘good girl’ to teachers.”

“Less respect for female staff vs male in behaviour—even with the same approaches they instantly listen to males more. More inappropriate jokes—racism, homophobic and sexist jokes with little consequences. Visible [and] audible dismissal/rejection of female staff to their faces when they appear to take classes.” 

These are quotes from a Monash University report which has cast light on the disturbing sexist conditions faced by teachers and students in primary and secondary schools across the country. 

Duty of Care: Teachers’ experiences of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment in Australian schools

 is based on the testimony of 2,600 educators and reveals the breadth and depth of the crisis. 

A common theme in the report is the lack of respect male students show female teachers. This includes frequent interrupting, ignoring of instructions, mocking and mimicking, speaking disrespectfully and refusing to accept responsibility when challenged about inappropriate behaviour. Physical aggression and intimidation were also reported, along with threats of more serious physical and sexual assault. Male students frequently make “derogatory comments toward females focusing on appearance and worth”, “jokes about gender roles e.g. the kitchen”, “inappropriate sexualised remarks about female bodies, including specifically about peers and/or staff” and “[making] sexual noises in the classroom” while female staff are trying to teach.

This behaviour is contributing to the burn-out of teachers in a profession already facing shortages due to poor pay and unmanageable workloads. One respondent put it clearly: “Being the front line and bearing the brunt of misogyny is exhausting and erodes self-worth”. According to the report, 77 percent of teachers say that sexism and misogyny have a “negative” or “very negative” impact on their wellbeing, and more than 50 percent of female teachers report that they either “occasionally” or “frequently” consider leaving the profession because of it. And the situation is getting worse—both primary and secondary teachers reported that gendered violence on the part of students had increased significantly in the previous twelve months.

Given adult teachers are feeling undermined, threatened and belittled by male students’ behaviour, the impact on teenage girls should be cause for immediate action. According to the report, “Younger students are comfortable using misogynistic language without thought e.g. calling girls in class a ‘slut’ ‘whore’ because they won’t share a highlighter”, and “Women/girls in class are okay with being treated with misogyny as this is seen as ‘normal’ now. They do not retaliate and internalise, making emotional regulation hard”. Another teacher observed: “Female students are scared to speak out and express their opinions in class with males who chastise them. I am noticing students are very hesitant to participate in discussion these days whereas it used to be female students being quite eager to share ideas and answer questions. Female students appear angrier than in the past as well”.

Male students direct sexist and misogynistic language towards their female peers freely, entrenching a toxic gender divide among students. Again, the statistics bear this out, with 80 percent of respondents agreeing that the behaviour is having a negative impact on student wellbeing. In observing and being victim to male students’ sexism—including constantly disrupting learning and making spaces hostile—girls are being socialised to accept dehumanising language and treatment and to make themselves small targets by withdrawing and accommodating to the selfish and anti-social behaviour of boys. 

And though there are undoubtedly some who are willing to challenge their peers’ appalling behaviour, it is an unacceptable environment for female students to be expected to navigate every day, while at the same time trying to do the actual tasks of deciphering Shakespeare or learning calculus. It is well established that students learn best when they feel safe, supported and respected. This is currently not the case for female students at Australian schools.

author: Rachel Evans
title: Inaugural Dr Adnan Al-Bursh lecture pays tribute to Gaza’s health workers
content:
More than 200 people attended the inaugural Dr Adnan Al-Bursh Memorial Lecture on October 17, hosted by Australian Healthcare Alliance for Palestine and Nurses and Midwives for Palestine.

The lecture aims to pay tribute to those who use their knowledge and expertise to demand human dignity, justice and freedom.

Al-Bursh, a prominent Palestinian orthopaedic surgeon and head of orthopaedics at Al-Shifa Hospital in the Gaza Strip, was born on September 17, 1974. He was tortured to death at the Ofer Prison in the Occupied West Bank and died on April 19, 2024 — just 50 years of age.

A striking image of Al-Bursh, by Mandy King, was displayed at the front of the meeting.

Dr Sarah Abdo, a consultant endocrinologist who chaired the event, said Al-Bursh was arrested by Israeli Defense Forces in late 2023, while working at Al-Awda Hospital. He was tortured for more than four months.

Abdo referred to the struggle to free Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, a Palestinian neonatologist and paediatrician. He was the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital, in Beit Lahia, in northern Gaza. Abu Safiya is being held in the same prison where Al-Bursh was murdered.

Renown cardiologist and Palestine justice supporter Professor Peter Macdonald gave the keynote address. Dr Ruth Mitchell, Dr Nada Abu Al-Rub and civil liberties lawyer Nick Hanna also addressed the meeting. Mitchell and Abu Al-Rub have both undertaken medical missions in Gaza.

Macdonald was stood down from St Vincent’s Hospital for two months in October last year, after a Zionist group complained about remarks he made in a personal capacity that cast doubt on allegations that Iran was behind arson attacks in Naarm/Melbourne and Sydney.

The University of Melbourne also cancelled Macdonald from his invitation to deliver a memorial lecture in honour of cardio-thoracic surgeon John Clarebrough. He was also suspended from his work with the Condoblin Aboriginal Health Service.

Apart from Macdonald’s work as a senior cardiologist in the Cardiopulmonary Transplant Unit at St Vincents, he is a Conjoint Professor of Medicine at the University of New South Wales and co-head of the Transplantation Research Laboratory at the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute.

Macdonald helped pioneer the transplant of donor hearts, which he addressed in his presentation. He spoke about the injustice of First Nations communities having to battle unequal health outcomes. “I am honored to give this lecture in memory of Al-Bursh. The conditions of medical staff in Gaza is indescribable. Their dignity and courage in face of this inhumanity is astounding.”

Macdonald urged people to read The Weight of Witness: The Experiences of Australian and New Zealand Medics in Gaza, to better understand the situation in Gaza.

Abu Al-Rub said: “The situation for people in Gaza is horrendous. They are bombing every day. Doctors, patients and families are all forced to live under canvas. Doctors work and because no-one has homes, they just sleep at the hospital. There is no food, no water, no medicine. Even baby formula is forbidden. I was not even allowed to bring in peanut butter into Gaza because it is ‘too nutritious’.”

“The blockade has turned life itself into a crime,” Abu Al-Rub said. “We must speak up … we cannot be complicit.”

Mitchell, a paediatric and adult neurosurgeon, undertook a medical mission to Gaza in May. “We have to continue, even if the movement to free Palestine seems at a lower ebb,” Mitchel said. “The ceasefire is in name only.”

Hanna congratulated Macdonald for resisting his suspension and continuing to speak out for Palestine. “We can’t forget South Lebanon,” he added. “Families living in rubble who, when you ask them, was it worth the sacrifice, they don’t falter in their support for Palestine.”

author: CMI Argentina
title: Se registró una nueva caída del empleo formal en julio: 9085 trabajadores perdieron su puesto
content:
Según datos del Sistema Integrado Previsional Argentino (SIPA), analizados por el investigador del Instituto de Estudios y Formación de la CTA – Autónoma Luis Campos, suman ya 14 meses consecutivos de retroceso del empleo en el sector privado. Agrega que julio fue el mes de mayor destrucción desde noviembre del año pasado, y que en el último año se destruyeron más puestos que en el primer año y medio de gobierno de La Libertad Avanza.


Foto: Indymedia Trabajadoras/es


“La fase de destrucción de empleo formal en el sector privado ya tiene la misma magnitud que la que se produjo en los últimos dos años del gobierno de Cambiemos. La gran diferencia es que en ese momento el sector público funcionaba como amortiguador. Ahora no. A nivel sectorial no se salva nadie, ni siquiera los ganadores del modelo. En el último año minería y petróleo e intermediación financiera destruyeron empleo formal. Agro y pesca tuvieron una suba marginal. Por el contrario, industria y comercio se desplomaron”, detalla Luis Campos.


Agrega que en lo que va de la gestión de La Libertad Avanza el empleo formal solo creció en Neuquén y Río Negro. Entre ambas provincias sumaron 16.723 trabajadores, mientras que en las 22 restantes perdieron su puesto casi 285.000 personas.


“En julio creció bastante el empleo en el sector público, pero posiblemente se trate de un tema metodológico. Había caído fuerte en junio, recuperó todo el deterioro en julio. Contra noviembre de 2023 acumula un retroceso del 2,5%, bien por debajo del sector privado. En casas particulares el empleo formal también cayó en julio, pero como tendencia general parece haberse estabilizado en los niveles de principios de 2025 luego de una caída muy fuerte en los cinco años anteriores”, señala.


En cuanto a los sueldos, Campos explica que el salario real relevado por el SIPA perdió un par de décimas contra la inflación en julio: “Parece haberse estancado a partir de marzo en niveles similares a los de noviembre de 2023. No parece haber ninguna razón para que repunte en el corto plazo”.


“En agosto la Encuesta de Indicadores Laborales registró una caída marginal. Por lo pronto, no hay ninguna señal de que el empleo formal vaya a recuperarse. Veremos hasta cuándo resisten las modalidades refugio, si es que ya no empezaron a agotarse”, finaliza el investigador.
