author: ROAPE
title: Fanon’s continuing presence and revolutionary Sudan
content:
Each generation must out of relative obscurity discover its mission, fulfil it, or betray it.


– Frantz Fanon,

The Wretched of the Earth

, 1968


I do not come with timeless truths … Every human problem must be considered from the standpoint of time.


– Frantz Fanon,

Black Skin, White Masks

, 2008


 


Introduction


Fanon was very aware of his time. And yet one hundred years after his birth, he remains strangely present, as if we are repeating the same history, the long durée of the unfinished anticolonial revolutions (see Gibson 2021). Published in 1961, Fanon’s last book,

The Wretched of the Earth

, is a product of his experience and reflections on Africa’s anticolonial struggle, including its first crisis in the Congo in 1961. Written as an intervention and addressing the readers as comrades, Fanon introduces the colonised challenge to the colonial world not as a rational confrontation of points of view, ‘but the untidy affirmation of an original idea propounded as an absolute’ (Fanon 1968, 41). Aware that colonialism carved up the continent into colonial fiefdoms, Fanon recognised that while the social struggle takes on a national form, it would inevitably degenerate into the regional, ethnic and racial lines often promulgated by colonial rule

if

 it did not put into practice a ‘minimum humanist’ programme (Fanon 1968, 163).


Challenging the imperial countries who speak of humanism but kill human beings wherever they find them, Fanon ends the book returning to the question of rehumanising the world, ‘For Europe, for ourselves, and for humanity, comrades, we must turn over a new leaf, we must work out new concepts, and try to set afoot a new [hu]man’ (Fanon 1968, 316). This was his idea of African liberation. Yet, on the hundredth anniversary of Fanon’s birth, not only has Africa become proportionately poorer and more unequal over the past 30 years but the post-independence ‘wa-Benz’, the newly embourgeoisified African ruling elites or simply ‘new whites’ (Nzongola-Ntalaja 2012, 40) – the ‘little greedy caste … with the mind of a huckster, only too glad to accept the dividends that the former colonial power hands out to it’ (Fanon 1968, 175) – keep reappearing.


While often dismissed as an advocate of violence rather than a thinker of African liberation, what is often elided in discussions of Fanon’s thought is the connection between the necessity of violence against settler colonies and Fanon’s criticisms of the military and the need for demilitarisation. This article focuses on what an engagement with Fanon’s thought could offer Sudanese revolutionaries. Understanding such an engagement dialectically, Fanon emphasised the importance of subjectivity in the ‘situation’ (and what Fanon also called the ‘lie of the situation’ (see Fanon 2018, 525)), which takes on a specific perspective because the Sudanese revolution involved millions of people in a non-violent revolution against military rule. It is this movement for life and liberation that must not be forgotten in the face of the reality of a counter-revolutionary military civil war that has led to daily human catastrophe for the Sudanese people.


While the Sudanese revolution began as a rejection of military rule, regional and world powers, including the United Nations (UN), have played a significant role in supporting the so-called civilian partnership of the Transitional Military Council, established in 2019, and have continued to support the armed forces following the 2021 military coup. The repeated failure of ‘international diplomacy’, notes Muzan Alneel (2023a), ‘is mainly due to the counter-revolutionary doctrine that animates its participants’.

1


The first section of this article discusses Fanon’s idea of demilitarisation and decolonisation. The second section, on the Sudanese revolution, discusses the importance, and legacies, of the resistance committees, while the final section returns to Fanon’s idea of revolutionary humanism in the praxis of anticolonial organisations.


National military or African solidarity through a corps of volunteers?


Fanon’s idea of an African legion was proposed in his speech delivered in December 1958 at the First All-African People’s Conference in Accra, Ghana. In an article in the Algerian National Liberation Front’s

El Moudjahid

title: Συγκεντρώσεις αλληλεγγύης στον παλαιστινιακό λαό, την Τετάρτη 7/10
content:
Την Τρίτη 7/10 συμπληρώνονται τρία χρόνια απο την έναρξη της αιματηρής γενοκτονίας του παλαιστινιακού λαού από το κράτος – δολοφόνο Ισραήλ και τη συμμαχία του με τις  ΗΠΑ και το ΝΑΤΟ. Πάνω απο 75.000 νεκρούς παλαιστίνιους των οποίων το 1/3 αποτελούν παιδιά μετράει η γενοκτονία η οποία 3 χρόνια μετά βρίσκεται ακόμα σε εξέλιξη και το Ισραήλ και οι ΗΠΑ συνεχίζουν την προσπάθεια καθολικής επίθεσης στις χώρες της Μέσης Ανατολής. Την ίδια μέρα, σωματεία, οργανώσεις και συλλογικότητες καλούν σε συγκεντρώσεις αλληλεγγύης στον παλαιστινιακό λαό, σε διάφορα σημεία της χώρας, διαδηλώνοντας ενάντια στην γενοκτονία και κατοχή της Γάζας από το κράτος – δολοφόνο Ισραήλ αλλά και στη πιστή συμμετοχή του ελληνικού κράτους σε αυτήν.


Καλέσματα:


Αθήνα, στις 18.00, στο Πάρκο Ελευθερίας


Θεσσαλονίκη, στις 19.00, στο Άγαλμα Βενιζέλου


Καρδίτσα, στις 19.00, στη κεντρική πλατεία


Ηράκλειο, στις 19.00, στη πλατέια Λιονταριών


Αθήνα:


Πρωτοβουλία Αλληλεγγύης στον Παλαιστινιακό Λαό Εργατικών Σωματείων και Συλλογικοτήτων –

Ένωση Παλαιστινίων Εργαζομένων Ελλάδας


Τρία χρόνια από την εισβολή στη Γάζα – Καμία συνενοχή | 7/10, 6μμ, πάρκο Ελευθερίας


Καμία σιωπή. Αλληλεγγύη στον Παλαιστινιακό λαό


Όλοι/όλες στη συγκέντρωση την Τετάρτη 7 Οκτώβρη 2026, ώρα 6μμ., στο πάρκο Ελευθερίας και στην πορεία προς τις Πρεσβείες ΗΠΑ και Ισραήλ


Η

Πρωτοβουλία Αλληλεγγύης στον Παλαιστινιακό Λαό Εργατικών Σωματείων και Συλλογικοτήτων

 καλεί τους εργαζόμενους, τους συνταξιούχους, τη νεολαία και τα συνδικάτα σε μαζική κινητοποίηση την Τετάρτη 7 Οκτώβρη 2026, με αφορμή τη συμπλήρωση τριών χρόνων από την έναρξη της εισβολής στη Γάζα του κράτους-δολοφόνου του Ισραήλ. Διαδηλώνουμε για να απαιτήσουμε τον άμεσο τερματισμό της γενοκτονίας του παλαιστινιακού λαού, το τέλος της κατοχής και την πλήρη απεμπλοκή της Ελλάδας από το σφαγείο στη Μέση Ανατολή.


Τρία χρόνια μετά την 7η Οκτώβρη 2023, ο Παλαιστινιακός λαός βρίσκεται αντιμέτωπος με μια άνευ προηγουμένου συστηματική προσπάθεια εξόντωσης και εθνοκάθαρσης. Τα επίσημα στοιχεία του Γραφείου Συντονισμού Ανθρωπιστικών Υποθέσεων του ΟΗΕ (OCHA) αποτυπώνουν το μέγεθος της φρίκης: πάνω από

74.900 νεκροί

 Παλαιστίνιοι -στη συντριπτική τους πλειονότητα γυναίκες και παιδιά- και περισσότεροι από

174.000 τραυματίες

, ενώ χιλιάδες παραμένουν θαμμένοι κάτω από τα συντρίμμια.


Στη

Γάζα

, το κράτος του Ισραήλ έχει ισοπεδώσει σχεδόν το σύνολο των ζωτικών υποδομών: νοσοκομεία, σχολεία, δίκτυα ηλεκτροδότησης, σταθμοί αφαλάτωσης και αντλιοστάσια νερού έχουν καταστραφεί ολοσχερώς. Ο πληθυσμός στερείται ακόμη και το πιο βασικό ανθρώπινο δικαίωμα, την πρόσβαση σε πόσιμο νερό και τροφή, αντιμετωπίζοντας έναν τεχνητά επιβεβλημένο λιμό και την εξάπλωση επιδημιών.


Την ίδια στιγμή, το σιωνιστικό κράτος κλιμακώνει τον πόλεμο και στην κατεχόμενη

Δυτική Όχθη

. Με πάνω από 1.000 νεκρούς, καθημερινές πολύνεκρες στρατιωτικές επιδρομές σε καταυλισμούς προσφύγων (Τζενίν, Τουλκάρμ), αθρόες κατεδαφίσεις σπιτιών, βίαιους εκτοπισμούς ολόκληρων κοινοτήτων και πάνω από 1.600 καταγεγραμμένες επιθέσεις φασιστών εποίκων με την κάλυψη του ισραηλινού στρατού, επιχειρείται η de facto προσάρτηση των παλαιστινιακών εδαφών.


Αυτό το διαρκές έγκλημα δεν θα μπορούσε να συντελεστεί χωρίς την ενεργή στήριξη, χρηματοδότηση και τον εξοπλισμό του Ισραήλ από τους ιμπεριαλιστές. Οι

ΗΠΑ

, το

ΝΑΤΟ

 και η

Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση

 δεν κάνουν απλώς «πλάτες» στο κράτος- δολοφόνο, αλλά αποτελούν συνενόχους πρώτης γραμμής.


Με αμύθητα πακέτα στρατιωτικής βοήθειας, διαρκή αποστολή οπλικών συστημάτων και διπλωματική ασυλία, η Ουάσιγκτον και οι Βρυξέλλες νομιμοποιούν την εθνοκάθαρση στο όνομα της δήθεν «αυτοάμυνας» του Ισραήλ, εξυπηρετώντας τα δικά τους γεωστρατηγικά και οικονομικά συμφέροντα στη Μέση Ανατολή.


Η γενοκτονία του Παλαιστινιακού λαού έχει και τη σφραγίδα όπως έχει και τη σφραγίδα της

Ελληνικής Κυβέρνησης

, που προχωρά σε περαιτέρω εμβάθυνση της στρατιωτικής συνεργασίας με το κράτος-δολοφόνο του Ισραήλ, επιβεβαιώνοντας το ρόλο της ως τοπικού τοποτηρητή των αμερικανονατοϊκών σχεδιασμών. Στα τέλη του Αυγούστου, μάλιστα, η

κυβέρνηση Μητσοτάκη

 υπέγραψε στο Τελ Αβίβ την απαράδεκτη διακρατική συμφωνία για την «

Ασπίδα του Αχιλλέα

», με προϋπολογισμό άνω των

3 δισ.

 ευρώ (που σε βάθος χρόνου αναμένεται να φτάσουν τα

5 δισ.

 ευρώ), με τη γιγαντιαία συμμετοχή ισραηλινών αμυντικών εταιρειών.


Για την

Πρωτοβουλία Αλληλεγγύης στον Παλαιστινιακό


Λαό Εργατικών Σωματείων και Συλλογικοτήτων

, η επιλογή αυτή αποτελεί ακόμη ένα βήμα στρατιωτικής πρόσδεσης …

author: Soreti Kadir
title: Finfinnee is the Third Space
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial centre of Addis Ababa. Being only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine. 


Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation of our relationship to ‘Ethiopia’, as a national identity, came up. It’s important to note that I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the “Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia” and the official establishment of a transitional government. 


This eventually led to the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) monopolizing power within the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a process that resulted in the isolation of those seeking political power within the EPRDF through the ballot. Given the size and economic importance of the Oromia region, it was the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), amongst others, that became a key target of political violence, creating political communities in exile exactly like the one that I grew up in.


I inherited a different definition of Ethiopia, coloured by memories and experiences of violence and displacement that informed my relationship to the state as a place of unbelonging for those who shared my identity. The day that the conversation with these two new friends wandered into political territory, we all engaged passionately, striving to reflect the extent of both our personal experiences and hopes for our country. They found my reflections to be overly nostalgic and antagonistic towards the country’s future.  Unconcerned for the good of the future. I found their insistence that we shared a national identity to be inaccurate and offensive. We agreed on little, and I found it exhilarating. 


That evening, I was restlessly anticipating the opportunity to tell my mother about what I thought was the most exciting experience of my trip to date. In recounting the story, I almost gave my mother a heart attack. Angry, afraid, and in shock, my mother warned me sternly against ever engaging in such conversation in public again. She asked me many questions about who these men were, how I knew them, and if we’d ever had such conversations before. What I was blind to, and what was the daily lived experience of my parents, was that Addis Ababa, primarily but not exclusively, was a heavily surveilled city, the State looking for the people doing exactly what I found myself doing that day – discussing the political reality of our country. Thereafter, I was careful, out of curiosity more than fear (being 16 with a high risk tolerance will do that), and refrained from fully-fledged conversations, opting for quiet enquiry when the opportunity presented itself. Although our conversation never veered down the road of politics again, I continued to visit my friends every day and remember rushing to say a heartfelt goodbye on the day I was due to fly back to Australia. 


For this piece, I will centre the discussion on Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, as opposed to extending the conversation to other parts of the country which exist with their own nuances and political realities, requiring more space for analysis than I have here. I share the introductory anecdote to forward the idea that, in Ethiopia, to nurture spaces of connection, community-building, and care, we must first invest in collective repair of the damage wrought by decades of state surveillance that has defined the range and breadth of relational life the city space can hold, and from the legacy of what can only be defined as settler colonialism. ‘Where’, figuratively and literally, can this process of repair take place? I argue that it must take place in Finfinnee, geographically the same location as Addis Ababa, but sociologically and …

author: Publicación Abierta
title: 12 de octubre: la conquista remata ahora la vida
content:
12 DE OCTUBRE: LA CONQUISTA REMATA AHORA LA VIDA


Por Rafael Bautista S.


La colonización ahora se propone


aniquilar al mundo entero, pues si no todos somos iguales,


la rebelión de las víctimas es el pecado


que hay que escarmentar,


porque dice Occidente: “toda la culpa la tienen las víctimas.


El verdugo es siempre inocente”.


Para los fines de la conquista, fue preciso, necesario y estratégico cercenar las memorias y ceremonias antiguas de los indios, porque en esos residuos de resistencia se reproducía su modo de vivir. La inversión religiosa la describe muy ben Guaman Poma de Ayala cuando señala que “les quitaron su ley antigua y les pusieron temor y culpa donde antes había justicia”. Para arrebatarles y despojarles de humanidad, no bastaba con reducirlos a la miseria sino acabar con su memoria y sus costumbres, con su historia y su cultura.


Pero lo que las armas habían pretendido terminar, sólo logró su aplazamiento, pues la memoria comenzó a renacer, una y otra vez que la amenaza del exterminio prendía sus terruños, pero también su rebeldía. Las armas jamás pudieron doblegar el espíritu de liberación que atravesó, hasta el día de hoy, todas las formas que adquirió la dominación, el despojo y el robo de su tierra sagrada.


Hoy la liberación se expresa como

restauración

. El “progresismo” no entiende que el progreso es un mito, que la alternativa ya no es aferrarse al tren del progreso sino ponerle un freno y proponerse, con mayor denuedo, despertar y

conservar

 los valores que la tradición de nuestros pueblos nos ha legado, frente al desastre y el desmoronamiento de los valores moderno-occidentales. Pero

restaurar

 no es volver sino

recrear

,

actualizar

 lo que hemos perdido: una existencia más digna, libre y justa, re-ligada a lo natural y espiritual, a la simpleza que significa vivir en plenitud; lejos del dinamismo, ritmo y la inclemencia del tiempo inhumano del capital y el mercado (una vida válida para todos, donde ya no gobierne la ambición de unos cuantos).


En el siglo XV, el Abya Yala estaba atravesando una época de esplendor civilizatorio, superior, en muchos casos, a la Cristiandad latino-occidental (porque Europa recién se estaba reconociendo como nueva entidad ontológica y geopolítica). En realidad, en 1492,

quien se descubre no es América sino Europa

 y lo hace no a partir del “encuentro” con el otro sino negando su humanidad, para afirmarse como superioridad absoluta, una vez que ha diezmado la capacidad de resistencia de los pueblos dominados. El Abya Yala no fue reducida civilizatoriamente por vivir en el atraso histórico, en la barbarie (que es una pura leyenda negra que está siendo desmentida, cada día, por los nuevos hallazgos y argumentos antropológicos, arqueológicos, demográficos, tecnológicos, etc., etc.).


No nos vencieron por astucia, inteligencia o superioridad sino por una incompatibilidad radical. La

cultura de la vida

 (en todas sus expresiones) respeta los límites éticos que manifiesta la idea del bien. Una cultura de muerte, basada en la culpa infinita, el sacrificio, la aniquilación del

humanismo del otro hombre

, no admite límite alguno. Como en la actualidad, cuando el Imperio y Occidente, en su decadencia, desatan la política del odio, desatan un poder sin límites. Salah ad-Dîn o Saladino lo expresaba así, refriéndose a los cruzados cristianos: es casi inhumano luchar contra ejércitos tan hambrientos de sangre y muerte. Si el monje Bernardo de Claraval estimulaba a los cruzados con el perdón de los pecados y el paraíso eterno, por cada moro que se aniquile, se comprende la crueldad que despierta el odio al “infiel”. Como hoy en Gaza, el Imperio y Europa jamás abandonaron esa brutalidad sin coordenadas morales. Los pueblos expulsados a ser periferia del “primer mundo”, fuera de las fronteras del

humanismo liberal-moderno excluyente y selectivo

, aun cargan con la interrogante: ¿cómo puede ser posible vivir en un mundo sin respeto por la vida?


Occidente nunca fue superior. Su moralidad los retrata en la figura de aquél que afirma que “lo único que puede detenerme es

Mi propia moral

,

Mi propio pensamiento

.

No necesito

 del derecho internacional”, Trump dixit. Occidente es el nicho de la tradición imperial, que siempre debe retornar, como dice Dostoievsky, al lugar del crimen. Es su condena y, por eso mismo, debe acallar a los vencidos, para dejar de escuchar el clamor de los muertos que deja su progreso y desarrollo.

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: From Haile Selassie to Abiy Ahmed: the Human Cost of Imperial Nostalgia
content:
The irony is difficult to escape. Haile Selassie became a symbol of resistance to foreign aggression while denying Eritreans the right to self-determination. Abiy Ahmed was rewarded for accepting Eritrea’s internationally recognized border, yet within a few years his government began advancing claims to sovereign access to the Red Sea. The very territorial settlement that helped earn him the Nobel Peace Prize now stands in tension with his maritime ambitions.

Both men benefited enormously from international recognition. Their reputations gave them prestige and influence, but those reputations have too often overshadowed the suffering of the people under their rule. Haile Selassie’s imperial government suppressed resistance in Tigray and annexed Eritrea. Under Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopia has endured devastating wars, while his government’s Red Sea rhetoric has renewed Eritrean fears of territorial aggression.

I have written about the dangers of romanticizing Ethiopia’s imperial past, most recently in Imperial Nostalgia: History, Sovereignty, and the Unfinished Work of Decolonization in the Horn of Africa. What concerns me today is that this nostalgia is no longer confined to history books or monuments. It has returned to contemporary politics, and the consequences could be catastrophic for another generation of Ethiopians and Eritreans.

Haile Selassie’s reputation rests heavily on his resistance to Italian fascism. His appearance before the League of Nations in 1936 became one of the defining moments of his international career. But the familiar account gives the emperor far more prominence than the people who actually fought the occupation.

Haile Selassie left Ethiopia in 1936 and spent the following years in Britain. Meanwhile, Ethiopian patriots remained behind, fighting a brutal occupation. They lived in the mountains, organized resistance, endured enormous hardship and risked their lives. The emperor became the international face of their struggle, but he was not the one carrying its daily burden.

Consider Belay Zeleke, one of the patriots who fought the Italians. After the emperor returned to power, Belay came into conflict with the imperial government. In January 1945, he was executed alongside his brother and other associates. Think about the irony. A man who had fought foreign occupation was hanged under the authority of an emperor celebrated around the world for resisting that same occupation.

The emperor’s record in Tigray reveals another contradiction. In 1943, when people in Tigray rose against imperial authority during the first Woyane uprising, Haile Selassie turned to Britain for military assistance. British Royal Air Force aircraft bombed Mekelle and other locations. As Human Rights Watch documented, British air power helped suppress resistance to the imperial government.

Here was an emperor celebrated for standing against European aggression using European aircraft against people resisting his own rule. How does that fit the image of a champion of freedom?

Haile Selassie’s reputation as a Pan-Africanist also deserves scrutiny. His role in establishing the Organization of African Unity in Addis Ababa in 1963 was important. But diplomatic achievement should not be confused with a consistent commitment to African freedom.

Haile Selassie and his foreign minister, Ketema Yifru, worked to establish Ethiopia as a center of African diplomacy. Hosting the OAU gave the emperor enormous prestige. Yet the same government was denying Eritreans the right to determine their future.

Eritrea’s federal autonomy had been systematically dismantled before Haile Selassie annexed the territory in 1962. While the emperor was celebrated as a defender of African independence, Eritreans were beginning a liberation struggle that would last thirty years.

The OAU largely treated Eritrea as an internal Ethiopian matter. Its silence is especially striking when compared with Western Sahara. The organization admitted the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic despite Morocco’s fierce opposition. It was prepared to confront one African government over self-determination but failed to extend comparable recognition to Eritreans struggling against Ethiopian rule.

The romanticization of Haile Selassie reached extraordinary heights through the Rastafari movement. Emerging from racial oppression in Jamaica, the movement invested in the Ethiopian emperor with immense spiritual and political significance. For some Rastafarians, he became a …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: The latest on Gabriel Rockhill’s “Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?”
content:
Controversy, controversy…it’s no surprise that this book is selling very well. See more on this from

Bisharat Abbasi

, in his post: “

In Defence Of Gabriel Rockhill’s

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism: Anti-Imperialist Marxism Versus The Imperial Theory Industry

.

“


DIGEST: Reviews, interviews, appearances


Marx Memorial Library

in London hosted a dual book launch for

Requiem for French Theory

 and

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?

with Gabriel Rockhill, Aymeric Monville, and Jennifer Ponce de León, who engaged in a discussion regarding the effects of imperialism on the production and dissemination of knowledge. Far from simply engaging in a critique of the faux radicalism of the prominent discourses within the imperial theory industry, the discussion was grounded in a reasoned defense of the vibrant international tradition of anti-imperialist Marxism. Topics included the imperial promotion of Western Marxism and postmodern French Theory, the international war of ideas, the failed efforts to discredit anti-imperialist Marxism, culturalism and identity politics vs. a materialist analysis of the colonial question, fascism past and present, the dialectics of actually existing socialism, and the current state of global class struggle in theory and practice.

Watch here

or below


The Left Chapter

, reviewed by Leo Schwarz:


“Shortly before his death, Herbert Marcuse wrote an essay on Rudolf Bahro’s book

The Alternative in Eastern Europe

. In the essay, Marcuse hailed Bahro’s ‘critique of actually existing socialism’ as ‘the most important contribution to Marxist theory and practice in decades.’ This statement was part of a coordinated campaign for the book and for Bahro that swept through the major media outlets of the Western world between 1977 and 1979–80. As we now know (or can know), a striking number of the key figures in this campaign maintained connections in the postwar decades to the Central Intelligence Agency or to various institutions and organizations that were either controlled, funded, or considered ‘friendly’ by the CIA or the U.S. State Department. In the first volume of his three-volume reconstruction of the ‘intellectual world war’ against actually existing socialism, Gabriel Rockhill examines the history and specific function of these networks of the ‘imperial theory industry’ that emerged after 1945, with his interest focused primarily on the Frankfurt School and the academic “Marxisms” of the Western world, which are usually categorized as ‘Western Marxism’…..”

 Read more….


Kaanan

,

 reviewed by Adel Samara


“…I was among those who criticized the Soviet system in its post-Stalin decades, and the lesson learned was that the greatest losers were the peripheral countries, especially the Arab nation, since the Soviets had long acted as a force restraining the imperialist beast. More importantly, this collapse was, in historical-materialist terms, a setback—an exception—because history fundamentally advances upward. Though our wounds were deep, the class enemy emerged victorious but also wounded, most notably by becoming the sole superpower, exposing its flaws and unleashing its brutality. In this brief context, I attempt to summarize Gabriel Rockhill’s book—a painstaking and rigorously documented scholarly work. Yet its timing is no less important than the work itself, for it constitutes a bold revolutionary confrontation that demonstrates the author’s profound communist commitment in an era when loyalty to communism has become rare and the fungi of internalized defeat have spread everywhere, filling the burrows with fleeing rats….”

title: Communiqué zur Velodemo vom 11. Oktober 2026
content:
Ein Jahr später. Wir alle sind wieder zurück und wir lassen uns weder von der Staatsgewalt, noch von der medialen und parlamentarischen Hetze gegen die kämpferische Palästina-Demo vom letzten Jahr einschüchtern!


Wenn wir uns die Strasse nehmen wollen, dann nehmen wir sie uns! Weil der Genozid in Gaza noch immer anhält, die Schweiz noch immer imperialistische Komplizin ist und weil der Widerstand gegen Imperialismus, Genozid und gegen ihren Krieg weiterhin als extremistisch geframed und kriminalisert wird.


Die antiimperialistische und antikapitalistische Velodemo startete beim Eigerplatz. Um 15:00 fuhren wir los und widersetzten uns der grossen Polizeipräsenz. Wir nahmen uns die Strassen und den Kreisel beim Eigerplatz und schon von Anfang an solidarisierten sich auch Menschen in Autos mit den Inhalten der Demo! Daraufhin fuhren wir auf die US-Botschaft zu, welche symbolisch für Trump und die US-imperialistische Tyrannei im Allgemeinen steht. Wenig überraschend wurden die umliegenden Strassen bereits von Robocops und Kastenwägen abgeriegelt. Wir führten unsere Smash-US-Imperialism Aktion deswegen mitten auf dem Bubenbergplatz durch.


Wir blockierten mit unseren Velos alle Strassen dieser grossen Kreuzung, und fesselten eine lebensgrosse Trump Figur an eine Säule.


Schliesslich luden wir Demonstrierende wie Passant*innen ein, Trump mit gefüllten Robidogsäckli, zu bewerfen bis er noch beschissener aussah als sonst schon!


Etwas später hörten wir eine Rede eines kurdischen Genossens, der für die kurdische Befreiung gekämpft hat.


Dabei sprach er über die PKK, welche den Aufbau des demokratischen Sozialismus und den 50-jährigen antiimperialistischen Kampf massgeblich vorangetrieben hat. Zudem betonte er die Wichtigkeit der Frauenbewegung, die eine führende Rolle im Kampf und beim Aufbau des demokratischen Sozialismus eingenommen hat. Die Frauenrevolution in Rojava und die Aufstände von Rojhilat unter der Parole Jin-Jiyan-Azadî (Frau-Leben-Freiheit) spielten eine Schlüsselrolle bei der weltweiten Verbreitung des kurdischen Frauenkampfes für Freiheit.

author: M. Reza Behnam
title: The Imperial Pen: Geopolitical Vandalism in West Asia
content:
For centuries, the lands stretching from the Levant to the Persian Gulf have been subjected to a strange form of conceptual alchemy. Driven by Western Orientalist scholarship, colonial cartography and modern geopolitical agendas, the dynamic, pluralistic mosaic of West Asia has been systematically reduced to a monolithic caricature, defined by violence, archaic fundamentalism, and in need of rescue.

These mutations are more than mere scholarly failures; they represent a destructive erasure of history. By denying complex societies their natural path toward modernity and stripping them of historical agency, these misrepresentations serve to validate existing systems of oppression.

To truly understand contemporary Arab West Asia, one must recognize that its political boundaries and power dynamics are essentially an imperialist artifact; and that it remains shackled to a modern version of the colonial 1916 Sykes-Picot ghost: artificial borders drawn by foreign pens, hyper-economies addicted to petrodollars, governance models built and local rulers chosen to appease external patrons and crush internal dissent.

British and French colonialists, Mark Sykes and Francois Georges Picot, engineered the systemic underdevelopment of West Asia, through calculated geopolitical vandalism. By secretly carving up Ottoman lands into European spheres of influence during World War I, with total disregard for demographic, tribal and economic realities, they deliberately trapped millions within artificial borders designed explicitly to facilitate trade routes and resource extraction at the expense of organic state-building and stability.

To maintain control and to serve the industrial demands of London and Paris, these external brigands thwarted local independence, weaponized sectarian and religious divisions, and essentially reduced entire societies into fractured resource-milked protectorates.

The Sykes-Picot Agreement and sibling treaties did more than redraw a map, they locked the region into ongoing instability. Imperial powers carved out unnatural states and installed local satraps—chronically fragile in legitimacy—willing to repress their own populations to stay in power and to carry out the bidding of their colonial overlords. This has left a consequential foundational legacy that the region’s people are forced to navigate today.

Even the conventional designation “Middle East” is a colonial byproduct; not born of indigenous geography. The imperialist term originated within the British India Office in the 1850s and gained public attention in 1902 when American naval strategist, Alfred Thayer Mahan, used it to describe the area around the Persian Gulf as a middle zone between the Near East and the Far East.

The Eurocentric label became official terminology during World War II after the British Armed Forces set up their Middle East Command in Cairo. In the 1950s, the United States integrated the term into official foreign policy, transforming a strategic naval calculation into a commonly accepted and used geopolitical descriptor.

Beyond the physical lines on a map, the legacy of imperialism endures in how borders drawn more than a century ago are understood and interpreted today.

When violence erupts in these states, Western discourse routinely defaults to essentialist tropes. They attribute the instability to “ancient ethnic, tribal or religious animosities” or an “inherent inability to govern,” rather than looking at the real roots of the conflicts.

Such oversimplified stereotypes are convenient fiction that absolve colonial powers of their historical responsibility. They conceal the ways in which modern authoritarian regimes, sectarian conflicts, religious factions and state collapses were systematically engineered, armed and manipulated by foreign powers seeking resource dominance and geopolitical control.

In his foundational critique of Orientalism, Palestinian-American scholar, Edward Said, demonstrated how Western academia, literature and media manufactured a false binary, framing the West as rational, logical and progressive, while painting the East as emotional, static and despotic.

In this construction, the people of West Asia are rarely permitted complexity as historical actors pursuing their own liberation, economic self-determination or social reform. Instead, they are filtered through reductionist archetypes; such as:

The fanatic: Driven solely by ancient grievances or religious dogma, entirely divorced from …

author: Wildcat #116
title: 1976 – 1991: Das Albartus-Papier der Revolutionären Zellen
content:
Die Jahre 1976 und 1991 markieren zwei deutliche Abstürze in der Geschichte der radikalen Linken in der BRD. Bezeichnenderweise kam Ende 1991 das Albartus-Papier der Revolutionären Zellen auf 1976 zu sprechen: die Flugzeugentführung von Entebbe. Anlässlich des 50. Jahrestags haben wir in der aktuellen Wildcat einen langen Artikel, der diese Verbindungen aufzudröseln versucht: »Entebbe und die Folgen«. Hier eine Kürzestfassung plus update:


Im Juni und Juli 1976 herrschte in Europa eine Hitzewelle. Die Temperaturen in Deutschland stiegen wochenlang regelmäßig über 30 Grad auf Spitzenwerte bis 36 und 37 Grad.


Politisch endete vor 50 Jahren das »rote Jahrzehnt«: 24. März 1976 Militärputsch in Argentinien. Am 9. Mai 1976 starb Ulrike Meinhof. Anfang Juni brach auf dem »Pfingstkongress« ein breiter Teil der radikalen Linken mit der Militanz und machte sich auf in die Institutionen. Am 10. Juli begann die Chemiekatastrophe in Seveso. Im August das Massaker von Tel al-Zaatar. Am 6. Oktober der Militärputsch in Thailand.


Auch kulturell war 1976 schlimm: ABBA »Dancing Queen«, Jürgen Drews »Ein Bett im Kornfeld«, Boney M. »Daddy Cool«. Kurz danach kamen dann die BeeGees »Stayin’ Alive« – der Sound zum Deutschen Herbst!


Für die deutschen Maoisten der diversen K-Gruppen lag 1976 zwischen dem Besuch von Franz Josef Strauß bei Mao (Januar 1975) einerseits, dem Krieg Vietnams gegen Kambodscha und den »Reformen« von Deng Xiao Ping (beides im Dezember 1978) andererseits. Die meisten fielen vom Glauben ab, viele von ihnen gründeten die Grüne Partei, andere später die Antideutschen. Diese eroberten nach 1991 die Hegemonie in der radikalen Linken.


Die Flugzeugentführung nach Entebbe…


Seit Anfang 1976 eskalierte der libanesische Bürgerkrieg. Nach monatelanger Belagerung stürmten Falangisten am 12. August das Lager von Tel al-Zaatar und töteten Tausende palästinensische Flüchtlinge.


Im Zusammenhang damit entführte ein deutsch-palästinensisches Kommando aus RZ und PFLP-EO am 27. Juni 1976 ein Flugzeug nach Entebbe und forderte die Freilassung von politischen Gefangenen. In der Nacht zum 4. Juli befreiten israelische Spezialkräfte die meisten der Geiseln. Das wird von gewissen Kreisen bis heute als das beste Kommandounternehmen aller Zeiten bejubelt (etwa: »Mit der Geiselbefreiung von Entebbe zeigte Israel vor 50 Jahren, wie man den Terror bekämpft« Nius 2. Juli 2026). Benjamin Netanjahu, dessen älterer Bruder bei der Befreiungsaktion starb, hat seine gesamte politische Karriere auf »Entebbe« und den »Kampf gegen den Terrorismus« aufgebaut.


»Die Aktion von Entebbe wurde rasch zu einem Vorwand für verschiedene Akteure, die bislang mit dem Milieu der radikalen Linken verbunden waren, sich von Internationalismus und Antiimperialismus ganz zu lösen.« (Gerhard Hanloser: »Desaster mit Nachspiel«)


Wegweisend war der Anti-Repressionskongress des Sozialistischen Büros Anfang Juni (»Pfingstkongress«). Am Abschlusstag hatte der spätere Außenminister Joschka Fischer vor 20.000 Besuchern in der berühmten Römerberg-Rede mit seiner militanten Vergangenheit gebrochen. Später hat er – die Dinge chronologisch auf den Kopf stellend – auf seinem Weg ins Außenministerium immer mal wieder betont, »Entebbe« sei das Ereignis gewesen, das ihn vom Saulus zum Paulus gemacht habe. Dabei lieferte es nur nachträglich den Vorwand.


»Entebbe« ist bis heute wirkmächtig. Das sah man an den Dutzenden von Artikeln und mehreren Büchern, die zum 50. Jahrestag erschienen. Das sah man aber auch daran, dass im März 2023 Mitglieder der Entebbe-Spezialeinheit eine der schärfsten Kritiken an Benjamin Netanjahu in einem offenen Brief formulierten. Netanjahu opfere den Staat Israel und das israelische Volk für seine eigenen Interessen, diffamiere Demonstranten gegen die Justizreform als Anarchisten und alle, die ihn nicht unterstützen, als Terroristen; er hetze Israelis gegeneinander auf.


… und die beginnende Institutionalisierung der radikalen Linken


1976 hätte auch anders ausgehen können. Im Juli hatten Chemiearbeiter in Seveso gestreikt, um die Katastrophe überhaupt öffentlich zu machen – aber sie hatten nicht mehr die Macht wie Jahre zuvor, die Wirtschaftspolitik des Landes neu zu orientieren. Die massenhaften Schüler- und Studentenproteste in Soweto seit Juni waren größtenteils selbst organisiert und schienen politisch endlich eine Alternative zum ANC zu eröffnen. author: Brasil 247
title: Celso Amorim Warns of U.S. Interference in Second Round Elections
content:
Ambassador Celso Amorim, special adviser to the presidency on international affairs, warned of the risk that the United States could interfere in Brazil’s election process. He said the October 25 presidential runoff carries consequences that reach far beyond Brazil’s borders. In an interview with Tutaméia on Friday, the former foreign and defense minister discussed pressure from the Trump administration on Latin America, the challenges facing Brazilian sovereignty, and the importance of the country’s technological and military independence.

Amorim said Brazil holds a strategic position in the global balance of power, and that the country’s political decisions have ripple effects across the Global South and relations between major powers.

“What happens in Brazil will have an influence on the global balance itself,” he said.

The diplomat stressed that Brazilian sovereignty depends on maintaining diverse international relationships and avoiding dependence on any single power.

“In the complex world we live in today, sovereignty doesn’t mean isolation. It means having relationships with more than one country. It means diversifying your relationships. It means not depending on a single power in any sense, economically, socioculturally, or even militarily in terms of defense,” he said.

Amorim Calls Out Washington’s Pressure on Brazil

Asked about possible attempts by the Trump administration to interfere in Brazil’s election, Amorim said he believes the influence of certain U.S. political sectors on Brazil’s political landscape is real.

He said this interference doesn’t need to target voting mechanisms directly. It can take the form of diplomatic, economic and political pressure, along with support for Brazilian ideological movements.

The presidential adviser cited the tariffs imposed by the United States, diplomatic restrictions, and initiatives from sectors of the American far right as examples of actions that, in his view, go beyond the limits of a balanced bilateral relationship.

Amorim also referred to reports of attempts to send American representatives to Brazil to inspect the electoral system, calling the idea absurd.

In the diplomat’s assessment, strategic U.S. documents reveal an intention to reassert American dominance over the Western Hemisphere. He said these initiatives need to be analyzed together, not as isolated incidents.

Diplomat Sees Risk of Unprecedented Submission to the United States

Discussing the Bolsonaro family’s international positions, Amorim said that unrestricted access to Brazil’s strategic information by the United States would represent a profound break from the country’s diplomatic tradition.

The former foreign minister compared the current situation to U.S. interference in the 1964 military coup, recalling the role played by then Ambassador Lincoln Gordon and U.S. plans to provide military support to the coup plotters.

Amorim noted that even during the military dictatorship, Brazil at times took positions independent of Washington, including on nuclear policy, maritime issues, and recognizing Angola’s independence.

For Amorim, control over natural resources and strategic technologies sits at the center of today’s international disputes. He cited critical minerals and artificial intelligence as areas where Brazil needs to preserve its own decision making power.

He argued that sovereignty isn’t an abstract concept, but something directly tied to economic development and the population’s quality of life. As an example, he pointed to the creation of Petrobras and the importance of Brazil having its own oil production capacity, especially during periods of international instability.

China and Strategic Autonomy Take Center Stage

Amorim also discussed the growing rivalry between the United States and China and what it means for Brazil.

He said competition between major powers can create opportunities for countries that maintain autonomy in choosing their trade and technology partners. The diplomat noted that the expansion of economic ties between Brazil and China stems partly from China’s ability to offer competitive trade and investment terms.

He argued that Brazil should maintain relationships with multiple partners, without subordinating its decisions to the interests of either Washington or Beijing.

title: 2023 Operation Al-Aqsa Flood as resistance vs US-Israel
content:
“We cannot condemn the genocide in Palestine without also condemning the imperialist United States.”

Filipino activists remembered the Operation Al-Aqsa Flood three years ago as the day Palestinians amplified their stand against imperialism.

Led by the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), activists marched on October 7 to the US Embassy to remember the historic operation against Israeli occupation after decades of Palestinian oppression.

Carrying the Palestinian flag and placards with images of slain journalists in Gaza, they marched along Kalaw Avenue in Ermita, Manila to condemn the Israeli attacks despite the ceasefire that supposedly took effect on October 10, 2025.

During the program, Amirah Lidasan, secretary-general of Moro Christian People’s Alliance and co-chairperson of Sandugo Movement of Moro and Indigenous Peoples for Self-Determination, said, “Gaza is not the land of another people. Gaza belongs to the Palestinians who are struggling.”

In 2025, US President Donald Trump introduced the Gaza peace plan, also known as the “Board of Peace,” which saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza. It also includes an agreement to end the war.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, Israeli attacks since the October 7, 2023 Operation Al-Aqsa Flood have killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children. The actual death toll may be higher, as official records rely on documented deaths and do not account for those still missing or buried under the rubble.

Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) Chairperson and former Bayan Muna Rep. Teddy Casiño highlighted the US role in Israel’s attacks on Palestine by continuing to provide unconditional financial and military support

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) rely heavily on imported arms from the US which accounts for 69 percent of Israel’s weapon imports from 2019-2023.

“We cannot condemn the genocide in Palestine without also condemning the imperialist United States. Not only has Israel committed genocide in Palestine, but the United States has also attached Venezuela, Iran and Yemen, and is now there is possibility to attack Cuba,” Casiño said.

On January 3, the United States abducted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his spouse, Cilia Flores, following months of US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific that reportedly killed more than 100 people.

The Trump administration’s actions, which critics have condemned as violations of international law and Venezuela’s national sovereignty, reflect what the progressive groups describe as a longstanding pattern of US imperialism.

Despite the controversy surrounding the operation, the Trump administration insisted on its intention to “run the country,” further raising concerns over Venezuela’s sovereignty and the Venezuelan people’s right to self-determination.

Rev. Alan Sarte, secretary-general of the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association stressed the determination of Palestinians to continue fighting for their freedom, calling on people around the world to oppose imperialism and defend national sovereignty.

author: Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Family moves into Nuxalk village site Nusq’lst for the first time in 164 years
content:
The cabin in the ancestral village of Nusq’lst.

Submitted photo


Nestled in the lush coastal temperate rainforest of the Bella Coola Valley sits the ancestral village of Nusq’lst.


The last time someone lived at the historic Nuxalk townsite was in

1862

, as people’s forced removal from their homelands and the devastating smallpox epidemic emptied many traditional villages.


Now, 164 years later, three generations of a family are calling Nusq’lst home again. 


Kmalsuuncw (Orden Mack) and his mother Nuskmata turned what was originally planned as a hand-built hunting cabin into a permanent family home when Kmalsuuncw became a new father.


Building the cabin quickly became a family project, with Kmalsuuncw receiving advice on its construction from cousins, uncles and other supporters.


“We’ve received a lot of community support, and honestly, that’s been a really driving feature as to why we kept on going for as long as we did,” he said in an interview with IndigiNews. 


Kmalsuuncw notes the site holds much of his family’s origin story. The village site’s name Nusq’lst was his grandfather — Nuskmata’s late father’s — name. 


In 2020, construction originally began with the intention of becoming a hunting cabin — but that goal soon changed as Kmalsuuncw found out he was going to be a father. He felt called to provide for his growing family with the food, safety and shelter found in and around their ancestral home. 


“Right when I found out that my wife Jessica was pregnant,” he recalled, “we had to turn it from a cabin to more of a home.”


They call their cabin “Qiqti’s House” (baby’s house), a reminder that they’re the first in generations to raise children there.


“We’re not building this place for us,” he said. “We’re building it for them.”


A sustainable home during a housing crisis


Kmalsuuncw — a member of the Xats̓úll First Natiion who also has ties to Nuxalk and Tŝilhqot’in communities — has made Q’umk’uts (Bella Coola) his home for the past seven years.


He traces the cabin’s impromptu beginnings to a family gathering in Nusq’lst around 2019.


In the midst of a local housing crisis, with few housing options available to community members, building a sustainable home on the Nusq’lst village site became increasingly important to Kmalsuuncw — which he began to see as his “responsibility” to build on Nuxalk territories.


Kmalsuuncw’s mother Nuskmata

told Coastal First Nations

 that some of the last ancestors to live at Nusq’lst were her great grandmother Mary Sampson and her sister, and “so it’s really about returning home and reclaiming that place.” 


While building the cabin his mom handled the logistics while he did the construction and carpentry. Without carpentry training, he learned quickly as he was “thrown in” to the experience throughout the process.


“That was something I kind of had to learn along the way,” he said.


He credits a family friend, Dean Mecham, as the one who taught him about the process of logging and using the wood for the cabin build process.


Kmalsuuncw noted how around 85 per cent of work on the house was done by hand, with help from an Alaskan mill — an attachment for chainsaws that helps cut logs into long boards from trees they felled for the cabin’s foundation.


Out of care for the land, Kmalsuuncw said they only cut the trees needed for the cabin site, leaving it surrounded by the forest.


“I feel so connected to this place,” he said, “because of the way that we made sure to leave it.”


Nusq’lst memorial pole.

Photo by Dionne Phillips


Nusq’lst memorial pole.

Photo by Dionne Phillips


A communal effort to build


The mother-and-son team didn’t build their home alone, however. 


More than 200 community members helped out on the project, becoming a sort of communal event, Kmalsuuncw said proudly.


Even at the beginning of the seven year process he was surprised at the support that quickly emerged from the hereditary leadership.


“Once they heard what we were doing after community events, we had full … unanimous support,” he said.


He also commented on the openness his family has had with the community on their plans which has created support for the cabin’s construction. 


“Everybody knows what we’re doing,” he said, “and they’ve all been really supportive.”


Even a trip to the store would turn into a community update session, as many locals have been interested in the progress from the start.


The cabin’s location has now become a gathering …

title: „So kann man nicht mehr leben“: Auch in Portugal wird gegen steigende Lebenshaltungskosten und Wohnungsnot protestiert
content:
Dossier

 der Instagram-Plattform „Não dá mais para viver assim“ („So kann man nicht mehr leben“) und mehr dazu:


Nach Protesten am 10. und 15. Oktober schließen sich am Samstag, 17. Oktober die Kämpfe gegen Lebenshaltungskosten und für öffentliche Infrastuktur zusammen


Die von der CGTP einberufenen Demonstrationen begannen heute Vormittag in Porto, Coimbra und weiteren Städten. In Lissabon ist die Kundgebung für heute Nachmittag angesetzt.


„

Der D. João I-Platz in Porto, Schauplatz der jüngsten Demonstrationen für bezahlbaren Wohnraum, füllte sich am Samstagvormittag erneut mit Menschen – bei einer von der CGTP organisierten Demonstration, bei der verschiedene Forderungen auf der Tagesordnung standen, wie „Höhere Löhne, bessere Renten und öffentliche Dienstleistungen“ oder „Gegen den Anstieg der Lebenshaltungskosten“ und „Ein neuer Kurs für Portugal“. author: Julius Gavroche
title: The Encampment Movement against Evictions and Gentrification
content:
from the

CrimethInc.

 collective, 15/10/2026


A Report from Madrid and Barcelona


On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the

Occupy

 movement in the United States.


Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.


Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.


Anti-fascists gather to defend the housing encampment in Madrid’s Plaza del Sol, 2026.


The housing movement in Spain has a long and complex history. For any period that we might choose as a point of departure, there always exists a prior precedent that could serve just as well—so where we begin depends on how we wish to make sense of what is happening today, how we wish to narrate this story that is still being written in the streets. What follows, then, is an attempt, however insufficient and incomplete, to tell this story, in hopes that you can learn or be inspired by something from it and, in this way, become part of this story and build upon it wherever you live.


We could perhaps begin with the

15-M movement

, which erupted a decade and a half ago as part of the sequence of uprisings that unfolded across the globe in 2011. Encampments spread across Spain much as they have today, full of people clamoring for “

real democracy

.”


Whereas elsewhere, repression often put these movements to an unresolved end, in Spain, this movement culminated with the formation of several far-left political parties, including Podemos, as well as strong municipalist movements in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities. Today, these parties lie in ruins, while the municipalists have largely lost whatever power they once held. Ultimately, much like

Occupy Wall Street

 and the Arab Spring, the true legacy of this sequence remains ambiguous, contested, and open to interpretation. Perhaps the 15-M movement is not the beginning of the story we’re telling, but simply the ruins from which the current one is being told.


Riot police are covered in eggs and paint while attempting to evict a building in Barcelona, 2021.


The movement that is now swelling across Spain emerged as a result of strong and stable union-style organizations that operate apart from the official institutional structures that are otherwise so present and influential in political life here. These organizations were built to tackle the housing crisis using horizontal and grassroots power, while simultaneously driving widespread and popular mobilizations like those we are witnessing today. These unions are novel in that they don’t involve questions of work directly, but rather address the conditions in which we live. The movement’s most significant antecedents lie in the creation of organizations such as the PAH (Platform for People Affected by Mortgages), the first chapter of which was founded in Barcelona in 2009. Like the more recently created housing organizations, the PAH groups practice what we call “social unionism.”


The premise is simple: an individual problem like a person facing the threat of losing their home is transformed into a collective issue addressed through shared political action. A variety of union-style tactics soon began to emerge, leading to the halting of many imminent evictions.

People cling to one another tightly, locked arm in arm, crowding in front of the door of the building’s entrance while several vans of riot police pull up and park nearby as scheduled. There’s an announcement from a police loudspeaker to the effect that people must disperse, but no one does. Eventually, the cops move in, struggling to pull each person away one by one …

author: Progressive International
title: When the Bargain Breaks
content:
On 23 September, Spanish police evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for 71 years. After buying her flat, property company Urbagestión had sought to increase Abascal’s rent to more than her monthly pension. Neighbours had prevented three previous attempts to evict her. The fourth succeeded. Abascal was carried out of her home on a stretcher and taken to hospital. The eviction was lawful.

Tens of thousands marched through Madrid in outrage. Protesters occupied Puerta del Sol, erecting more than 1,200 tents, complete with named streets and a makeshift medical centre. They demanded rent controls, protection against eviction and an end to housing speculation. Parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November. On 7 October, Abascal died in hospital, one day before she was due to sign an agreement allowing her to return home.

Across the Pyrenees, a protest that began at a secondary school in a Paris suburb has become a national uprising. Lycée Saint-Exupéry was missing 13 teachers, a deputy head and essential support staff. Students and teachers walked out. Within days, blockades and other disruptions had spread to more than 1,000 schools. At Lycée Paul-Éluard in Saint-Denis, students described rats in the corridors, collapsing ceilings, windows sealed for fear they would fall on pupils, and one nurse for 2,000 students.

On 6 October, over 250,000 people marched across France, as teachers, parents, trade unions and university students joined the school children. Police used tear gas and made hundreds of arrests. The government promised 3,000 substitute teachers, but the protests continued. As one student put it: “We ask for teachers, they send us police.”

On the Indian subcontinent, 6,000 kilometres away, the capital city of Delhi is under siege by its own government. The Modi regime deployed nearly 35000 police to lockdown the city against student protests. More than 2.2 million students sat the national medical entrance examination in May, competing for far fewer places. When questions were found to have circulated in advance, the examination was cancelled. Students who had spent years preparing, and families who had spent their savings supporting them, erupted in anger.

These unemployed graduates and disenchanted youth called themselves the Cockroach Janta Party, reclaiming a disparaging remark from the Chief Justice about unemployed youth as a badge of pride. What began as an Instagram joke with an AI-generated cockroach logo became a mass movement. In July, the protests forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. By October, the movement had joined the struggle against the removal of some 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, which critics accuse the Election Commission of manipulating to benefit Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.

On 10 and 11 October, police and paramilitary forces sealed roads, closed metro stations and detained protesters demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Denied access to Jantar Mantar, Delhi’s designated protest site, demonstrators regrouped at markets, intersections and flyovers across the capital.

In Albania, that fire was sparked from a stretch of barbed wire. This May, developers fenced off access to the coast at Zvërnec, where a luxury resort backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner threatens the protected Vjosa-Narta wetlands. Villagers produced property deeds and a 2013 court ruling recognising their claim to the land. When residents and environmental activists confronted the development, private security guards dragged them away.

The injustice struck a nerve. The capital, Tirana, has repeatedly been brought to a standstill by protestors carrying inflatable flamingos, the birds whose habitat the development threatens, declaring that “Albania is not for sale”. The protests grew into a revolt against corruption and the grip of oligarchs on the country’s economy and political system. This week, tens of thousands of students protesting over education and living costs have joined the movement, with clashes leaving dozens injured and arrested. Footage is circulating on social media of citizens being abducted into unmarked vans. Prime Minister Edi Rama refuses to resign.

title: Kocaeli’de yurttaşlar ev ve iş yerlerindeki suyu kendi imkanlarıyla tahliye ediyor
content:
İzel Gözde Meydan [email protected]

Kocaeli’de yağışların yol açtığı su baskınları yaşamı olumsuz etkilerken, yurttaşlar ev ve sitelerine dolan suları kendi imkanlarıyla tahliye etmeye çalışıyor.

Değirmendere Topçular Mahallesi’ndeki 1919 Sitesi halkı; siteyi, bina içlerini ve zemin kattaki evlerin tamamını su bastığını söyledi.

Site halkından bir yurttaş, ilgili kurumlara yaptıkları başvurulara yanıt alamadıklarını ifade ederek yaşadıklarını şöyle anlattı:

“Dün gece 12’den bu yana aramadığımız kurum kalmadı. Ne belediyeler ne AFAD, itfaiye kimse gelmedi. Kendi imkanlarımızla pompalarla suyu tahliye ediyoruz. Benim evimin salonunu tamamıyla su bastı. 20 dakikada bir kontrol ediyoruz. Çünkü yeniden su basıyor.”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: NSW Socialists launch campaign with a bang!
content:
“Our message is clear: the working class isn’t going to take this shit lying down anymore”, roared Ryan Chapman, NSW Socialists candidate for the seat of Wollongong, at the launch of the party’s 2027 state election campaign.

The 300-strong crowd burst out in applause. The venue, Ashfield Town Hall, was packed to capacity.

The speakers, three of the party’s six lower-house candidates, reflected Australia’s modern, multicultural working class. The first speaker, Alma Torlakovic, candidate for the Western Sydney seat of Granville, spoke movingly of her childhood in war-torn Bosnia and Croatia. Shovan Bhattarai, candidate for the inner-west seat of Newtown, humorously described the multicultural lunchtimes at her Western Sydney primary school. Chapman spoke of growing up working class on the South Coast and joining the navy as his only option.

The housing crisis was a recurring theme. Chapman spoke about the campaign to defend the Bellambi housing estate north of Wollongong. Labor MP for the area and state planning minister Paul Scully wants to knock down the estate because it is on prized beachfront property. After detailing the eye-watering average rent rises in the inner-west, Bhattarai explained the party’s housing policy of slashing rents by 35 percent, implementing a rent freeze and building 150,000 new public housing units.

Housing is a clear example of how the NSW Labor government screws over workers to protect the profits of the rich. Labor is happy to take workers’ votes, but once in government, the party, in Torlakovic’s words, “treat Western Sydney like garbage”. The crowd was full of boos and cries of “shame” at any mention of federal or state Labor politicians.

“We are the party for the millions of people who make this city run”, declared Bhattarai. This unashamed emphasis on class politics is a refreshing antidote to a mainstream politics filled with either middle-of-the-road progressivism or vitriolic far-right bile.

After the speeches, people stuck around for food, drinks and campaign strategising. New volunteers met the campaign managers in their electorates, and people signed up for the numerous party activities planned for the coming weeks. The launch kicked off a frenetic fortnight of activity. Party activists hope this will help firmly establish the party among prospective voters and meet more people who will join the movement.

While we may not be backed by billionaires or the mainstream media, the socialist movement has always been fuelled by endless enthusiasm and dedication combined with a radical vision of a better world. If you want to be a part of that, get involved with the campaign today.

author: Javier Moreno Zacarés
title: Fifteen Years Later
content:
Fifteen years after the indignados occupied the Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s central plaza is once again the locus of a mass movement that has brought Spain to a political impasse. How are we back here again? The immediate trigger was the eviction of an elderly tenant. Maricarmen Abascal, who had occupied her rent-capped apartment in central Madrid since 1956, was expelled from her home on 23 September after the investment fund Urbagestión acquired the property and exploited a legal loophole to quintuple her rent. Maricarmen’s age and vulnerability – the 87-year-old was removed on a hospital bed and has since died – made it a particularly egregious breach of the moral economy. The case struck a nerve, prompting a political storm; the government has now announced a snap election. As protests spread nationwide, the encampment at Puerta del Sol consolidated under the leadership of the Sindicato de Inquilinas, Madrid’s tenant union. Media outlets are reporting on the motions passed at the open-air general assembly. One decision has been of particular public interest: a general strike for the right to housing, announced for 11 November, a few weeks before the election.

The political elite faces a reckoning. At the outset of the current parliamentary term in 2023, the progressive coalition headed by Sánchez’s centre-left Socialist Party (PSOE) placed housing at the top of the agenda. The promises were ambitious: the provision of mass social housing, the imposition of rent controls, the reassertion of the public interest against rentier logics. Yet these commitments yielded little. This was partly due to the obstruction of the right, both in parliament and in the regional governments under its control. But a share of the blame lies in the ambivalence of the Socialist Party itself, whose ministers have repeatedly expressed discomfort with what they regard as excessive regulation of housing. The junior coalition partner Sumar, a nebulous alliance of progressive parties, has proven feeble in holding the Socialists to account. They are now also a target of the protests, who charge the entire governing alliance of complicity with the rentiers. Amid the fury in the streets, Sumar’s cabinet members hastened to pressure the Socialist housing minister, Isabel Rodríguez – herself a landlord who owns multiple properties – to approve emergency measures to block evictions and institute permanent rolling contracts, both key demands of the tenant unions. Last Friday, both measures were struck down in parliament, to the anger of the masses gathered outside.

That a recalcitrant right-wing opposition – comprising the conservative People’s Party (PP) and the far-right Vox – would block the measures was entirely predictable. What was less so was that the deciding vote would be cast by an ally of the government: the centre-right Junts, party of the Catalan-nationalist bourgeoisie. The vote revealed a peculiarity of the Spanish conjuncture. Though the right-wing bloc is the largest in parliament, it is divided along nationalist lines, fractures the government has exploited – drawing support from the Catalan right to keep the Spanish unionist right out of power. It was always an unstable arrangement, premised on nation trumping class. On the housing question, the plurinational right voted in alignment with its shared interests (Junts has the largest proportion of landlords in parliament).

The Spanish right now enjoys a comfortable lead in the polls, which point to a PP–Vox coalition if elections were held tomorrow. But the wind is blowing in an uncomfortable direction for them. Over the past week, public opinion has swung massively in favour of regulating house prices, even among a slim majority of right-wing voters. In a matter of days, the protests have shifted the national conversation away from the right’s preferred talking points of crime and migration, overwriting a summer of hysteria around the border crisis in Ceuta. They have also deflected attention from the corruption scandals afflicting PSOE: only last June, a former minister in Sánchez’s cabinet was sentenced to twenty-four years in prison for influence-peddling related to substandard Covid-19 face masks. Ever the survivor, Sánchez has seized the moment with a characteristically audacious move. He has framed the election on 29 November as a plebiscite on the housing question, shifting the blame for it onto the right and boldly appealing to the electorate to ‘subdue the elites’ …

author: anred
title: «12 de Octubre, nada que celebrar»: pueblos originarios marchan contra los desalojos y la extranjerización de la tierra
content:
Marcha del Contrafestejo del 12 de octubre de 2024. Foto: archivo Nicolás Parodi / Página 12


Bajo la consigna “¡Nada que celebrar, muchas luchas que sostener!”, la Organización de Comunidades y Pueblos Originarios (ORCOPO) convocó a una marcha y contrafestejo para este lunes 12 de octubre, a las 18, en Plaza de los Dos Congresos. La jornada de lucha denunciará el avance de los desalojos, la criminalización de las comunidades indígenas, la extranjerización de la tierra, los proyectos extractivistas, la entrega, el saqueo y el despojo, en un escenario de creciente conflictividad territorial luego del reciente fallo de la Corte Suprema. La convocatoria se da en el marco de la confirmación judicial del desalojo de la Lof Inalef, en Río Negro, y una nueva amenaza contra la Lof Melo, en Neuquén. Ambos casos se suman a otros conflictos territoriales que atraviesan comunidades originarias en distintas regiones del país y que, para las organizaciones indígenas, evidencian una ofensiva sobre sus territorios en paralelo con el desmantelamiento de herramientas de protección y la reactivación de la derogación de la Ley de Tierras Rurales. También exigen justicia por Rafael Nahuel y libertad para quienes permanecen detenidos por luchar.

Por ANRed.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: French Gov't Cracks Down on Mass Protests over Cost of Living, Education Cuts; 2,400+ Arrested
content:
Hundreds of thousands of protesters marched in over 140 cities across France on Saturday, demanding relief from the high cost of living, more funding for public services and improvements to deteriorating schools, among other grievances. The demonstrations were the latest — and largest — in a series of protests that began in September with high schooler-led demonstrations against overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure. Some cities saw property destruction, arson and theft on Saturday, with city halls and other symbols of the state coming under attack. Officials said nearly 1,000 police officers were injured and some 2,400 people were arrested.


“What is frustrating to see is how little the police violence is addressed and talked about, which is really the main violence and the real violence today that is taking place in France,” says Rayyan Seriket, a member of the French student union.


“We’re talking about shattered jaws, high schoolers and adolescents who have been blinded,” adds Harrison Stetler, an independent journalist and teacher based in Paris.


This all comes as Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally party is leading in the polls six months ahead of France’s elections. “This situation is essentially what Marine Le Pen hopes for,” says Stetler.

title: Συγκεντρώσεις αλληλεγγύης σε διωκόμενους/ες, την Τρίτη 20/10
content:
Το πρωί της Τρίτης 20/10 πραγματοποιούνται δύο συγκεντρώσεις αλληλεγγύης σε διωκόμενους/ες αγωνιστές/τριες. Στις 09.00, στο Εφετείο Λάρισας, ο αγωνιστής Κώστας Α., αντιμετωπίζει πρωτόδικη καταδίκη 3,5 ετών για τη συμμετοχή του στις μεγάλες κινητοποιήσεις ενάντια στην καύση απορριμμάτων από την ΑΓΕΤ-Lafarge και ο συντονισμός συλλογικοτήτων Βόλου μαζί με οργανώσεις καλούν σε συγκέντρωση ενάντια στη δίωξη του. Παράλληλα, την ίδια ώρα στα Δικαστήρια Ευελπίδων, θα πραγματοποιηθεί συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στις 3 διωκόμενες που συνελήφθησαν και κατηγορούνται για επίθεση στο Διοικητικό Εφετείο Αθηνών.


Καλέσματα:


Στις 09.00 στα Δικαστήρια Λάρισας, δίκη σε 2ο βαθμό του αγωνιστή Κ.Α.


Στις 09.00 στα Δικαστήρια Ευελπίδων, συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στις διωκόμενες της 25/04


Αναλυτικά:


Δικαστήρια Λάρισας:


Συντονισμός Συλλογικοτήτων Βόλου


Δε θα μας δικάσουν οι δολοφόνοι της ΑΓΕΤ – Lafarge


Να αθωωθεί ο διωκόμενος αγωνιστής Κ.Α.


Όλες/οι στο εφετείο της Λάρισας την Τρίτη 20/10 στις 09:00


Η διαδήλωση της 13ης Ιουνίου 2020, έξω από το εργοστάσιο της ΑΓΕΤ, ενάντια στη καύση σκουπιδιών, αποτέλεσε και αποτελεί μέχρι σήμερα την κορυφαία στιγμή του μεγάλου κινήματος του λαού της πόλης του Βόλου, να ζήσει σε μια πόλη χωρίς το διαρκή αργό θάνατο της καύσης σκουπιδιών.


Το σύνθημα «Να φύγει η Lafarge», που κυριάρχησε εκείνη την περίοδο, αποτέλεσε μια ώριμη διεκδίκηση μιας χρόνιας διαδικασίας αντιπαράθεσης τόσο γύρο από την καύση σκουπιδιών, όσο και εν γένει γύρω από την ύπαρξη του εργοστασίου της ΑΓΕΤ ουσιαστικά μέσα στον αστικό ιστό της πόλης. Αποτέλεσε την ανάταση και κλιμάκωση της λαϊκής απαιτητικότητας, που έπαψε να πείθεται από τα παραμύθια περί «ελέγχου των ρύπων» και διεκδικούσε επι της ουσίας το λόγο για την ίδια την πόλη που ζούμε, κόντρα στο καθεστώς τοποτηρητή της ΑΓΕΤ – Lafarge.


Αυτή τη λαϊκή ανάταση επιχείρησε να υποτάξει η γενικευμένη κατασταλτική επιχείρηση που κορυφώθηκε τον Ιούνη του 2020 με το βασανισμό και την κρατική δολοφονία του Βασίλη Μάγγου. Το κατασταλτικό κρεσέντο περιελάβανε, το άγριο χτύπημα της μεγάλης διαδήλωσης έξω από την ΑΓΕΤ, η οποία απαρτιζόταν από κάθε ηλικιακή ομάδα, με τόνους χημικών και χρήση βίας. Την καταδίωξη πολλών διαδηλωτών χιλιόμετρα μακριά από το εργοστάσιο της ΑΓΕΤ, σε κεντρικούς δρόμους της πόλης του Βόλου και τη ρίψη χημικών ακόμα και μέσα στο τμήμα επειγόντων περιστατικών του νοσοκομείου Βόλου. Την άγρια βία το ίδιο βράδυ έξω από την Αστυνομική Διεύθυνση Μαγνησίας, σε πολίτες που συγκεντρώθηκαν εκεί ως ένδειξη αλληλεγγύης στους συλληφθέντες της διαδήλωσης, με αποτέλεσμα τον σοβαρό τραυματισμό δεκάδων. Το λυσσώδη ξυλοδαρμό και βασανισμό του Βασίλη Μάγγου την επόμενη της διαδήλωσης (14/06), έξω από τα δικαστήρια της πόλης, μέσα στο αστυνομικό όχημα που τον μετέφερε, αλλά και στο αστυνομικό τμήμα, που είχε σαν συνέπεια τον βαρύτατο τραυματισμό του (6 σπασμένα πλευρά και τραύματα σε ζωτικά όργανα), που σχετίζεται και με το θάνατό του 1 μήνα μετά. Τη γκανγκστερικού τύπου εισβολή σε σπίτια διαδηλωτών τις επόμενες ημέρες για «συλλογή στοιχείων». Τη δημιουργία μιας σειράς κατασκευασμένων διώξεων σε 15 συνολικά διαδηλωτές και διαδηλώτριες. Την πρωτοφανή και χυδαία μεταθάνατο δίωξη του ίδιου του Βασίλη Μάγγου.


Συνέπεια των παραπάνω ήταν να κατασκευαστούν φαιδρές αστυνομικές και διωκτικές σκευωρίες που οδήγησαν σε ένα πολύχρονο κύκλο δικών, στις οποίες οι εν λόγω σκευωρίες κατέρρευσαν με απόλυτο τρόπο, με αποτέλεσμα την αθώωση της συντριπτικής πλειοψηφίας των εμπλεκόμενων αγωνιστών και αγωνιστριών. Μέρος αυτών των μεθοδεύσεων είναι και η δίωξη του αγωνιστή Κ.Α., που του χρεώθηκαν κατηγορίες ακόμη και σε βαθμό κακουργήματος. Αν και πρωτόδικα, το Δεκέμβρη του 2024, η διωκτική σκευωρία κατέρρευσε με πάταγο, καθώς το δικαστήριο έκρινε αθώο τον Κ.Α. για το κακούργημα της χρήσης εκρηκτικών υλών και για τα πλημμελήματα της οπλοχρησίας και της πρόκλησης βαριών σωματικών βλαβών, τον έκρινε όμως ένοχο για τα πλημμελήματα της διατάραξης κοινής ειρήνης, της βίας κατά υπαλλήλων και της οπλοκατοχής, καταλογίζοντας του την ποινή των 3,5 χρόνων φυλάκισης.


Με ακραία εκδικητική κατεύθυνση εισαγγελέας και δικαστές εξάντλησαν τα ποινικά όρια για τις εν λόγω κατηγορίες, αρνούμενοι να δεχτούν οποιοδήποτε ελαφρυντικό, αδιαφορώντας πως στην ακροαματική διαδικασία δεν αποδείχτηκε καμία από τις πράξεις που καταλογίζονταν. Η πρωτόδικη απόφαση αποτύπωσε τη σαφή κατεύθυνση του αστικού συστήματος να καταδικάσει ανθρώπους των κινημάτων και να τους εμπλέκει σε πολύχρονους και πολυέξοδους δικαστικούς αγώνες, για …

title: Größter Protest gegen Tunesiens Präsident Saied seit Jahren: In Tunesien fallen immer wieder Strom und Wasser aus, Medikamente und Lebensmittel sind knapp
content:
„… Tausende Menschen haben in der tunesischen Hauptstadt Tunis gegen Präsident Kais Saied demonstriert. Es ist der größte Protest gegen seine Herrschaft seit Jahren. Die Demonstrierenden warfen Saied vor, die Demokratie zu untergraben und die Wirtschaftskrise im Land zu verschärfen. Zu der Kundgebung am Samstag hatten die Gewerkschaft UGTT und Bürgerrechtsgruppen aufgerufen. Oppositionsparteien des gesamten politischen Spektrums schlossen sich an, außerdem Ärzte, Anwälte und Journalisten – dass sich so viele unterschiedliche Gruppen hinter einem Ziel vereinen, ist in Tunesien eher ungewöhnlich. Die Demonstrierenden forderten die Freilassung inhaftierter Kritiker des Präsidenten und riefen Parolen wie »Keine Angst, die Macht gehört dem Volk« und »Die Gefängnisse sind voll, die Menschen hungrig«…“

 und mehr daraus:

Die Opposition bezeichnete diesen Schritt als Staatsstreich. Menschenrechtsorganisationen werfen dem Präsidenten außerdem vor, verschärft gegen die Zivilgesellschaft, Journalisten und politische Gegner vorzugehen. Ärzte und Menschenrechtsgruppen berichteten von Todesfällen und von einem Anstieg von hitzebedingten Einweisungen in Krankenhäuser. Auch Häftlinge hätten schwer zu leiden gehabt. Statt Informationen bereitzustellen, seien die Behörden hart gegen Demonstrierende vorgegangen. Die jetzige Demonstration fand auf der Avenue Habib Bourguiba statt. Die Straße war ein zentraler Ort der Proteste im Jahr 2011, die maßgeblich zum sogenannten Arabischen Frühling führten.“
